Induction for extended affine type A A Soergel bimodules from a maximal parabolic
Marco Mackaay, Vanessa Miemietz, Pedro Vaz

Abstract
. In this paper we take a first step towards the categorification of the Zelevinsky tensor product of finite dimensional representations of extended affine type A A Hecke algebras.



1.
Introduction

This paper is part of our ongoing study of the birepresentation theory of extended affine type
A_{n-1}
Soergel bimodules in characteristic zero, which
we started in
[
MMV
]
. The monoidal category of these Soergel bimodules, denoted
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
in this paper, was studied both algebraically and diagrammatically in
[
MaTh
]
and
[
Eli2
]
, and categorifies the extended affine type
A
Hecke algebra
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
.
This algebra is infinite dimensional, which on the categorical level corresponds to the fact that

\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
is not finitary but
wide finitary
, in the terminology of
[
Macph
]
.
Whereas finitary birepresentation theory of finitary monoidal categories/bicategories, such as Soergel bimodules of finite Coxeter type, is fairly well developed, see e.g.
[
MMMTZ1
]
and

[
MMMTZ2
]
and references therein, birepresentation theory of wide finitary monoidal categories/bicategories is still in its infancy. Some fundamental results in finitary birepresentation theory
were generalized to the wide finitary setting by Macpherson in
[
Macph
]
, but his framework does not cover triangulated birepresentations, which play a prominent role in the birepresentation
theory of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
. For example, the evaluation birepresentations of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
in
[
MMV
]
are triangulated. In this paper, we continue our study of the birepresentation theory of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
, taking a first step towards the categorification of parabolic induction. As the reader will see, this also involves triangulated birepresentations.

Parabolic induction and restriction play an important role in the finite dimensional representation theory of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
.
In particular, for any integers
1\leq k<n
, there is a well-known embedding of algebras

(1)

\psi_{k,n-k}\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n},

which is the analog of the embedding of finite symmetric groups
\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mathfrak{S}_{n-k}\to\mathfrak{S}_{n}
.
Given two finite dimensional representations
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
, respectively,
one can use
\psi_{k,n-k}
to define their
Zelevinsky tensor product

(2)

M_{1}\odot M_{2}:=\mathrm{Ind}_{\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}}^{\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}}M_{1}\otimes M_{2},

which is a finite dimensional
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
-representation. Zelevinsky
[
Zel
]
classified the
finite dimensional irreducible representations of the extended affine type
A
Hecke algebra in terms of combinatorial
objects called multisegments. Leclerc, Nazarov and Thibon
[
LNT
]
gave a necessary and
sufficient condition for irreducibility of
M_{1}\odot M_{2}
, based on the multisegments corresponding to two finite dimensional irreducible representations
M_{1}
and
M_{2}
.

Now, let
k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}
such that
k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}=n
(assuming that
n\geq 3
, of course). Then one can show that

(3)

\psi_{k_{1}+k_{2},k_{3}}(\psi_{k_{1},k_{2}}\otimes\mathrm{id}_{\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{3}}})=\psi_{k_{1},k_{2}+k_{3}}(\mathrm{id}_{\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{1}}}\otimes\psi_{k_{2},k_{3}}),

which implies that there is a canonical isomorphism

(4)

\left(M_{1}\odot M_{2}\right)\odot M_{3}\cong M_{1}\odot\left(M_{2}\odot M_{3}\right),

with
M_{i}
being a finite dimensional representation of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{i}}
for
i=1,2,3
.
If we define the embedding of algebras

\psi_{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{1}}\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{2}}\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{3}}\to\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}

as either one of the two composite maps in (
3
), then
M_{1}\odot M_{2}\odot M_{3}
can also be
defined directly as

\mathrm{Ind}_{\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{1}}\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{2}}\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{3}}}^{\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}}M_{1}\otimes M_{2}\otimes M_{3},

which by the above is canonically isomorphic to either one of the two isomorphic representations in (
4
).

More generally, let
k_{1},\ldots,k_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}
such that
1\leq m\leq n
and
k_{1}+\ldots+k_{m}=n
. Then there is an
embedding of algebras

(5)

\psi_{k_{1},\ldots,k_{m}}\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{1}}\otimes\dotsb\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{m}}\to\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n},

which can be used to define the corresponding Zelevinsky tensor product

M_{1}\odot\dotsb\odot M_{m},

with
M_{i}
being a finite dimensional representation of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{i}}
for
i=1,\ldots,m
,
and this tensor product is associative up to canonical isomorphism. For more information on the Zelevinsky tensor product
and its role in representation theory, see
[
LNT
]
and references therein.

In this paper, we initiate the categorification of the Zelevinsky tensor product. Specifically, we define a linear, monoidal functor

(6)

\Psi_{k,n-k}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\boxtimes\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})

which categorifies the embedding
\psi_{k,n-k}
in (
1
). Here
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
denotes the homotopy category of bounded
complexes in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
. Before continuing, we should note that
\psi_{k,n-k}
is
usually defined in terms of the Bernstein presentation of the extended affine type
A
Hecke algebra. Unfortunately, there is currently
no categorification of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
based on that presentation. The decategorification of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
is naturally associated to the Kazhdan-Lusztig
presentation of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
, so we define
\psi_{k,n-k}
in terms of that presentation and use it as the starting point for the definition of
\Psi_{k,n-k}
in this paper.
Note that in
[
StWe
]
, the authors use the categorification of parabolic induction for finite type
A
Soergel bimodules, where the analog of
\Psi_{k,n-k}
is much easier to define and does not involve Rouquier complexes.

The way to categorify the Zelevinsky tensor product using
\Psi_{k,n-k}
is a bit roundabout, because we do not know how to make sense of
something like

\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}\boxtimes_{\,\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\,\boxtimes\,\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}}\mathbf{M}_{1}\boxtimes\mathbf{M}_{2},

where
\mathbf{M}_{1}
and
\mathbf{M}_{2}
are finitary birepresentations of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
, respectively. This would require an
analog of the balanced box tensor product for module categories over finite tensor categories, defined in
[
DaNi
, Section 2.7]
, which does not (yet) exist in our setting. Therefore, we follow a different approach, explained below. We first sketch the general idea and then point out some technical hurdles. Recall that, for a fiat bicategory
\mathcal{C}
(e.g. a linear additive pivotal category satisfying certain finiteness conditions), there is a correspondence between transitive finitary birepresentations of
\mathcal{C}
and algebra
1
-morphisms in (the abelianization of)
\mathcal{C}
, see
[
MMMT
, Corollary 4.8]
. Note that in that same paper, and subsequent ones like
[
MMMTZ2
]
, the correspondence was first formulated
with coalgebra
1
-morphisms, instead of algebra
1
-morphisms. For technical reasons,
we prefer algebra
1
-morphisms in this paper, see the comments below. Moreover, the bicategories in this paper have only one object and are hence monoidal categories, thus we speak about algebra objects. Any monoidal functor
\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
between monoidal categories maps algebra objects to algebra objects and can, therefore, be used to induce birepresentations of
\mathcal{C}
to birepresentations of
\mathcal{D}
, which is how we would like to go about categorifying the Zelevinsky tensor product. Unfortunately,
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
is not
finitary but wide finitary, and
\Psi_{k,n-k}
does not take values in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
but in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
.

In
[
Macph
]
, a correspondence between wide finitary birepresentations and (co)algebra
objects in some completion is given, but there is currently no analog for triangulated birepresentations. In the examples of finitary or triangulated birepresentations of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
that we fully understand, the algebra objects are typically given by countable coproducts of tensor products of Soergel bimodules and Rouquier complexes. Hence we introduce certain cocompletions of additive and triangulated monoidal categories/bicategories containing these
kinds of algebra objects/1-morphisms in
Section 5.2
, which are smaller than
the completions considered in
[
Macph
]
. To explain our preference for algebra objects over
coalgebra objects in this paper, note that algebra objects typically belong to cocompletions
whereas coalgebra objects typically belong to completions. As can be seen from our calculations in
Section 5.3
, cocompletions are easier to work with in practice. In
Section 5.3
we work out the explicit example of the categorified Zelevinsky tensor product
\mathbf{W}:=\mathbf{V}\boxdot\mathbf{V}
of the trivial finitary birepresentation
\mathbf{V}
of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{1}
with itself. Its construction is technically quite involved. We first define and analyse a wide finitary
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
-birepresentation
\mathbf{U}
corresponding to the algebra object
\mathrm{Y}:=\Psi_{1,1}(\mathrm{X}\boxtimes\mathrm{X}))
in the cocompletion of
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})
, where
\mathrm{X}
is the algebra object in the cocompletion of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{1}
corresponding to
\mathbf{V}
. Following the terminology introduced in
[
MMV
]
, we call
\mathbf{U}
a

wide finitary cover
of
\mathbf{W}
. To obtain a triangulated birepresentation,
we then observe that
\mathrm{Y}
induces a right action of
\mathbb{Z}^{2}
on
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})
which commutes with the left action of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
, so the
orbit category
\Omega
inherits the structure of a
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
birepresentation. We prove that
\mathbf{U}
is equivalent to the full subcategory
of
\Omega
whose objects can be identified with those of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
under the usual embedding into
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})
. In general,
the orbit category of a triangulated category under a group action does not inherit a natural triangulated structure, but in this case we can relate it (via a technical detour which we will explain in
Section 5.3.2
) to a triangulated orbit category using a dg-enhancement as
in
[
FKQ
, Theorem/Definition 1.1]
. By construction, this triangulated orbit category is a
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
birepresentation and we conjecture that its triangulated Grothendieck group is isomorphic to
W
, see
5.29
. It seems likely that this approach can be generalized, but we do not develop a general theory of these kinds of birepresentations and the corresponding algebra objects/1-morphisms in this paper, leaving that for future work.

Something else beyond the scope of this paper is the generalization of
\Psi_{k,n-k}
to a linear monoidal functor

\Psi_{k_{1},\ldots,k_{m}}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{1}}\boxtimes\dotsb\boxtimes\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{m}}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})

for
k_{1},\ldots,k_{m}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}
such that
1\leq m\leq n
and
k_{1}+\ldots+k_{m}=n
, categorifying (
5
). Conceptually it is clear how to define such a generalization, but we postpone the lengthy technical details to a future paper. Finally, to prove the categorical analog of (
3
), i.e., the existence of a natural isomorphism

\Psi_{k_{1}+k_{2},k_{3}}(\Psi_{k_{1},k_{2}}\boxtimes\mathrm{Id}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{3}}})\cong\Psi_{k_{1},k_{2}+k_{3}}(\mathrm{Id}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k_{1}}}\boxtimes\Psi_{k_{2},k_{3}})

for
1\leq k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}\leq n
such that
k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}=n
, we would first need to extend

\Psi_{k,n-k}
to a monoidal functor (with the same notation)

\Psi_{k,n-k}\colon K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k})\boxtimes K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k})\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}).

Proving the existence of such an extension is a non-trivial problem and is related to similar extension problems in other contexts, see

[
ALELR
, Conjecture 1.2]
,
[
Eli2
, Section 1.6]
,
[
ElHo
]
and
[
MMV
, Section 1]
. The solution of this problem is also a topic for future research.

2.
Parabolic embedding: decategorified story

Throughout the paper, let
n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}
. For
n=1
, the
affine Weyl group

\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{1}
of type
\widehat{A}_{0}
is the trivial group. Similarly, the finite Weyl group
\mathfrak{S}_{1}
of type
A_{0}
is the trivial group.

For
n\geq 2
, let
\widehat{I}:=\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}
and
I:=\{1,\ldots,n-1\}
. By a slight abuse of notation, we will often identify
\widehat{I}
with the set of representatives
\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}
and consider
I
as a subset of
\widehat{I}
.

For
n=2
, the
affine Weyl group
\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{2}
of type
\widehat{A}_{1}
is generated by the simple reflections
s_{0},s_{1},
subject to the relations

s_{i}^{2}=1,

for
i\in\widehat{I}
.

For
n>2
, the
affine Weyl group

\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
of type
\widehat{A}_{n-1}
is generated by the simple reflections
s_{i},\;i\in\widehat{I}_{n},
subject to the relations

s_{i}^{2}=1,\mspace{40mu}s_{i}s_{j}=s_{j}s_{i}\mspace{10mu}\text{if}\mspace{10mu}|i-j|>1,\mspace{40mu}s_{i}s_{i+1}s_{i}=s_{i+1}s_{i}s_{i+1},

for
i\in\widehat{I}
.

A
reduced expression (rex)
for an element
w\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
is a finite word

(s_{i_{1}},\ldots,s_{i_{m}})
of simple reflections, for some
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, such that
w=s_{i_{1}}\cdots s_{i_{m}}
and there is no word consisting of fewer simple reflections with that property. All rexes for
w
contain the same number of simple reflections, which is called the length of
w
and denoted by
\ell(w)
. By definition, the rex for the neutral element is the empty word of length zero (i.e.
m=0
).

The
extended
affine Weyl group
\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{\mathrm{ext}}
is the semidirect product

\langle\rho\rangle\ltimes\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n},

where
\langle\rho\rangle
is an infinite cyclic group generated by
\rho
and

\rho s_{i}\rho^{-1}=s_{i+1},

for
i\in\widehat{I}
. In particular, when
n=1
, the extended affine Weyl group
\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{1}^{\mathrm{ext}}
is just the infinite cyclic group
\langle\rho\rangle
.

The finite Weyl group of type
A_{n-1}
is the symmetric group on
n
letters,
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
, corresponding to the subgroup of
\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
generated by
s_{i},\;i\in I
.

2.1.
Hecke algebras

Let
q
be a formal parameter. For
n=1
, the
extended affine Hecke algebra

\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{1}
is simply the group algebra of
\langle\rho\rangle
over
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
.

For
n=2
, the
extended affine Hecke algebra

\widehat{H}^{ext}_{n}
is the
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
-algebra generated by
T_{0},T_{1}
, and
\rho^{\pm 1}
, subject to the relations

(7)

\displaystyle(T_{i}+q)(T_{i}-q^{-1})=0,\mspace{40mu}\rho\rho^{-1}=1=\rho^{-1}\rho,\mspace{40mu}\rho T_{i}\rho^{-1}=T_{i+1},

for
i\in\widehat{I}
.

For
n>2
, the
extended affine Hecke algebra

\widehat{H}^{ext}_{n}
is the
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
-algebra generated by
T_{i},\;i\in\widehat{I}
, and
\rho^{\pm 1}
, subject to the relations

(8)

\displaystyle(T_{i}+q)(T_{i}-q^{-1})=0,\mspace{40mu}T_{i}T_{j}=T_{j}T_{i}\mspace{10mu}\text{if}\mspace{10mu}|i-j|>1,\mspace{40mu}T_{i}T_{i+1}T_{i}=T_{i+1}T_{i}T_{i+1},

(9)

\displaystyle\rho\rho^{-1}=1=\rho^{-1}\rho,\mspace{40mu}\rho T_{i}\rho^{-1}=T_{i+1},

for
i,j\in\widehat{I}
. Note that
T_{i}
is invertible
for every
i\in\widehat{I}
:

T_{i}^{-1}=T_{i}+q-q^{-1}.

As is well-known,
\widehat{H}^{ext}_{n}
is a
q
-deformation of the group
algebra
\mathbb{Z}[\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}^{\mathrm{ext}}]
with the
standard basis
given by

\{\rho^{m}T_{w}\mid m\in\mathbb{Z},w\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}\}
, where
T_{w}:=T_{i_{1}}\cdots T_{i_{\ell}}

for any
reduced expression
(rex)
s_{i_{1}}\cdots s_{i_{\ell}}
of
w
.

Another presentation of
\widehat{H}^{ext}_{n}
is given in terms of the
Kazhdan–Lusztig generators

b_{i}:=T_{i}+q
, for
i\in\widehat{I}
,
and
\rho^{\pm 1}
, subject to the relations

(10)

\displaystyle b_{i}^{2}=[2]b_{i},\mspace{40mu}\rho\rho^{-1}=1=\rho^{-1}\rho,\mspace{40mu}\rho b_{i}\rho^{-1}=b_{i+1},

for
n=2
, and

(11)

\displaystyle b_{i}^{2}=[2]b_{i},\mspace{40mu}b_{i}b_{j}=b_{j}b_{i}\mspace{10mu}\text{if}\mspace{10mu}|i-j|>1,\mspace{40mu}b_{i}b_{i+1}b_{i}+b_{i+1}=b_{i+1}b_{i}b_{i+1}+b_{i},

(12)

\displaystyle\rho\rho^{-1}=1=\rho^{-1}\rho,\mspace{40mu}\rho b_{i}\rho^{-1}=b_{i+1},

for
n>2
, where
i\in\widehat{I}
and
[2]:=q+q^{-1}
. Note that
T_{i}=b_{i}-q
and
T_{i}^{-1}=b_{i}-q^{-1}
, for every

i\in\widehat{I}
. The
Kazhdan–Lusztig basis
is given by
\{\rho^{m}b_{w}\mid m\in\mathbb{Z},w\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}\}
, where the definition of
b_{w}
requires the choice of a rex for
w
but is independent of that choice.

For
n=1
, the (non-extended)
affine Hecke algebra

\widehat{H}_{1}
is the trivial one-dimensional algebra isomorphic to
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
. For
n\geq 2
, the (non-extended)
affine Hecke algebra

\widehat{H}_{n}
is the subalgebra of
\widehat{H}^{ext}_{n}
generated by either
T_{i}
or
b_{i},
for
i\in\widehat{I}
.

For
n=1
, the
finite Hecke algebra

H_{1}
is also the trivial one-dimensional algebra isomorphic to
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
. For
n\geq 2
,
the
finite Hecke algebra

H_{n}
is the
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
-subalgebra of
\widehat{H}_{n}
generated by either
T_{i}
or
b_{i}
, for
i\in I
.

There is a third presentation of
\widehat{H}^{ext}_{n}
, called the
Bernstein presentation
. In that presentation,
\widehat{H}^{ext}_{n}
is defined as a twisted tensor product of
H_{n}
and the algebra of Laurent polynomials in
n
indeterminates with coefficients in
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
. There are several possible choices for defining the commutation relations. The one we use here has indeterminates
y_{1},\dotsc,y_{n}
, with relations given by

(13)

T_{i}^{-1}y_{i}T_{i}^{-1}=y_{i+1},

for
i\in I
.

The relation between this Bernstein presentation and our first presentation of
\widehat{H}^{ext}_{n}
is
given by

(14)

\displaystyle y_{1}

\displaystyle=\rho T_{n-1}\dotsm T_{2}T_{1},

(15)

\displaystyle y_{i}

\displaystyle=T_{i-1}^{-1}\dotsm T_{2}^{-1}T_{1}^{-1}\rho T_{n-1}\dotsm T_{i+1}T_{i},\quad i=2,\ldots,n-1.

Remark 2.1
.

Some remarks about the various conventions in the literature are in order.
We try to follow conventions close to those in
[
Eli2
]
.
Our presentation of the extended affine Hecke algebra in
Section 2.1

agrees with
[
Eli2
]
, as does the relation between the standard generators and the
Kazhdan–Lusztig generators.

The
standard trace

\epsilon\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}\to\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
, which also plays an important role in this paper, is the

\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
-linear map defined by

(16)

\epsilon(\rho^{r}T_{w})=\delta_{r,0}\delta_{w,e},

for
r\in\mathbb{Z}
and
w\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
, where
\delta_{-,-}
is the Kronecker delta. The trace induces a
q
-sesquilinear form
(-,-)
on
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
defined by

(17)

(x,y):=\epsilon(\omega(x)y),

where
\omega
is the
q
-antilinear antiinvolution on
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
defined by
\omega(\rho)=\rho^{-1}
and
\omega(T_{w})=T_{w}^{-1}
, for

w\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
. By definition,
q
-sesquilinear means that
(-,-)
is
\mathbb{Z}
-bilinear and satisfies
(qx,y)=q^{-1}(x,y)=(x,q^{-1}y)
, for all
x,y\in\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
. The above definitions imply
that
\omega(b_{w})=b_{w^{-1}}
and that the Kazhdan-Lusztig basis is
asymptotically orthonormal
w.r.t.
(-,-)
, see
e.g.
[
EMTW
, Theorem 3.21]
for non-extended affine type A.

Theorem 2.2
.

For all
k,l\in\mathbb{Z}
and
u,v\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
, we have
\left(\rho^{k}b_{u},\rho^{l}b_{v}\right)=\delta_{k,l}\left(b_{u},b_{v}\right)
and

\left(b_{u},b_{v}\right)\in\begin{cases}1+q\mathbb{Z}[q],&\text{if}\;u=v;\\
q\mathbb{Z}[q],&\text{else}.\end{cases}

2.2.
The embedding

Let
1\leq k\leq n-1
. There are two unital embeddings of
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
-algebras
\psi_{L}\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\to\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
(the left embedding) and

\psi_{R}\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
(the right embedding), which are easily defined in terms of the Bernstein presentation:

\displaystyle\psi_{L}\colon\begin{cases}T_{i}\mapsto T_{i},\quad i=1,\dotsc,k-1,\\
y_{i}\mapsto y_{i},\quad i=1,\dotsc,k,\end{cases}

\displaystyle\psi_{R}\colon\begin{cases}T_{j}\mapsto T_{k+j},\quad j=1,\dotsc,n-k-1,\\
y_{j}\mapsto y_{k+j},\quad j=1,\dotsc,n-k.\end{cases}

The two embeddings
give rise to a
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
-linear map

\psi_{k,n-k}\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n},

defined by

\psi_{k,n-k}(a\otimes b):=\psi_{L}(a)\psi_{R}(b).

By definition,
\psi_{k,n-k}(a\otimes 1)=\psi_{L}(a)
and
\psi_{k,n-k}(1\otimes b)=\psi_{R}(b)
, where we denote the identity element of the various Hecke algebras by the same symbol
1
.

It is easy to see that this map is a homomorphism of algebras. Note that
\psi_{L}
and
\psi_{R}
form a
commuting pair of
algebra homomorphisms
, in the sense that

\psi_{L}(a)\psi_{R}(b)=\psi_{R}(b)\psi_{L}(a)

holds for all
a\in\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k},b\in\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
, because the
y_{m}
for
1\leq m\leq n
all commute with each other and we have
T_{i}T_{j}=T_{j}T_{i}
,
T_{i}y_{j}=y_{j}T_{i}
and
T_{j}y_{i}=y_{i}T_{j}
for all
1\leq i\leq k-1
and
k+1\leq j\leq n-1
.
Therefore, for all
a_{1},a_{2}\in\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and
b_{1},b_{2}\in\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
, we have

\psi_{L}(a_{1})\psi_{L}(a_{2})\psi_{R}(b_{1})\psi_{R}(b_{2})=\psi_{L}(a_{1})\psi_{R}(b_{1})\psi_{L}(a_{2})\psi_{R}(b_{2}),

which means that

\psi_{k,n-k}(a_{1}a_{2},b_{1}b_{2})=\psi_{k,n-k}(a_{1},b_{1})\psi_{k,n-k}(a_{2},b_{2}).

Using (
14
) to translate to the presentation in terms of the standard generators and
\rho
given in (
8
) and (
9
), yields

(18)

\displaystyle\psi_{L}({\rho_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}L}})

\displaystyle=y_{1}T_{1}^{-1}T_{2}^{-1}\dotsm T_{k-1}^{-1}=\rho T_{n-1}\dotsm T_{k},

(19)

\displaystyle\psi_{L}(T_{0})

\displaystyle=\psi_{L}({\rho_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}L}}^{\!\!\!\!-1}T_{1}{\rho_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}L}})=T_{k}^{-1}\dotsm T_{n-1}^{-1}T_{0}T_{n-1}\dotsm T_{k},

and

(20)

\displaystyle\psi_{R}({\rho_{{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}R}}})

\displaystyle=y_{k+1}T_{k+1}^{-1}T_{k+2}^{-1}\dotsm T_{n-k-1}^{-1}=T_{k}^{-1}\dotsm T_{1}^{-1}\rho,

(21)

\displaystyle\psi_{R}(T_{0})

\displaystyle=\psi_{R}({\rho_{{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}R}}}^{\!\!\!\!-1}T_{1}{\rho_{{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}R}}})=T_{0}\dotsm T_{k-1}T_{k}T_{k-1}^{-1}\dotsm T_{0}^{-1},

where we use the notation
{\rho_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}L}}
and
{\rho_{{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}R}}}
for the twist generators of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
, with
\rho
being used for the generator of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
. The underscript letters
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}L
and
\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}R
are meant to signify “
left
” and “
right
” to match their position in the tensor product
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
.

Since
\psi_{L}({\rho_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}L}})
and
\psi_{R}({\rho_{{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}R}}})
commute, we have

(22)

\psi_{k,n-k}({\rho_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}L}},{\rho_{{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}R}}})=T_{k}^{-1}\dotsm T_{1}^{-1}\rho\rho T_{n-1}\dotsm T_{k}=\rho T_{n-1}\dotsm T_{k+1}T_{k-1}^{-1}\dotsm T_{1}^{-1}\rho.

The image of the Kazhdan–Lusztig generators under
\psi_{L}
and
\psi_{R}
is

\displaystyle\psi_{L}(b_{i})

\displaystyle=b_{i},\quad i=1,\dotsc,k-1,

\displaystyle\psi_{R}(b_{j})

\displaystyle=b_{k+j},\quad j=1,\dotsc,n-k-1.

Using (
19
) and (
21
) it follows at once that

\displaystyle\psi_{L}(b_{0})

\displaystyle=T_{k}^{-1}\dotsm T_{n-1}^{-1}b_{0}T_{n-1}\dotsm T_{k},

\displaystyle\psi_{R}(b_{0})

\displaystyle=T_{0}\dotsm T_{k-1}b_{k}T_{k-1}^{-1}\dotsm T_{0}^{-1}.

2.3.
Diagrammatics

As is well known, the various Hecke algebras described above also have a diagrammatic incarnation, since all of them can be defined as a quotient of the group algebra of the corresponding braid group. In this incarnation, the standard generators correspond to crossings between two neighboring strands. In the affine case, we have to use braid diagrams on a cylinder, which we depict as a rectangle where the two vertical boundary components are identified. In this diagrammatic presentation for
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
we have

where
i=1,\dotsc,n-1
. Note that we don’t draw all the vertical lines and that the boundary points at the top, resp. at the bottom, of the braid diagram are cyclically ordered.
In our planar presentation we always order them from left to right starting with
1
and ending with
n
. In our conventions,
the product
XY
consists of gluing the diagram of
X
atop the one of
Y
.

The embedding
\psi_{k,n-k}
can also be described diagrammatically in a natural way. The diagram for
\psi_{k,n-k}(X\otimes Y)
consists of placing the cyclinder with the diagram for
Y\in\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
inside the cylinder with the diagram for
X\in\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and then projecting the outer cylinder over the inner in such a way that the boundary points of the diagram for
X
are sent to themselves, while the boundary points of the diagram for
Y
are sent to the points labelled
k+1,\dotsc,n
.
This is easily visualized using colored diagrams: we use
blue
for the diagrams of the elements of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and
purple
for the ones of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
. In this convention, the cylinder with a red diagram goes inside the one with blue diagram.

Note that the equation
\psi_{k,n-k}({\rho_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}L}}\otimes 1)\psi_{k,n-k}(1\otimes{\rho_{{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}R}}})=\psi_{k,n-k}(1\otimes{\rho_{{\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}R}}})\psi_{k,n-k}({\rho_{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}L}}\otimes 1)

translates to “
blue
and
purple
sliding past each other” in the corresponding compositions of the diagrams above.

3.
Rouquier-Soergel calculus

3.1.
Soergel calculus in extended affine type
A
and Rouquier complexes

In this section, we initially revisit the definition of the diagrammatic Soergel category for the extended affine type
A
as presented in
[
MaTh
]
(see also
[
MMV
]
and
[
Eli2
]
).

Let
\Bbbk
be an arbitrary field. Our conventions for graded (
\Bbbk
-linear additive) categories and shifts are as in
[
MMV
, §3.1]
, which match those of
[
EMTW
, Section 4.1]
. Since those conventions are important, let us briefly recall them.
Throughout this paper, graded will always mean
\mathbb{Z}
-graded. For any
t\in\mathbb{Z}
, the grading shift
\langle t\rangle
of a graded vector space
M\cong\oplus_{a\in\mathbb{Z}}M_{a}
is defined by
(M\langle t\rangle)_{a}:=M_{a+t}
for all
a\in\mathbb{Z}
. This implies that

\mathrm{hom}(M\langle r\rangle,N\langle t\rangle)
consists of all homogeneous linear maps between
M
and
N
of degree
t-s
. The graded
morphism space of all morphisms from
M
to
N
is defined as
\mathrm{Hom}(M,N):=\oplus_{t\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathrm{hom}(M,N\langle t\rangle)
.
In the categories of this paper, the objects need not be vector spaces, in which case the grading shifts are formal, but the morphism spaces are
always vector spaces consisting of (equivalence classes of) linear combinations of diagrams. Each diagram has some degree
s\in\mathbb{Z}
and can therefore be seen as a morphism between two objects with shifts
M\langle r\rangle
and
N\langle t\rangle
, such that
s=t-r
, or as a homogeneous morphism between
M
and
N
of degree
s=t-r
. To distinguish a non-graded category
\mathcal{C}
with
shift and lower case morphism spaces of the form
\mathrm{hom}(M\langle r\rangle,N\langle t\rangle)
from the associated graded category with morphism spaces of the form
\mathrm{Hom}(M,N)
, we
denote the latter by
\mathcal{C}^{*}
.

Recall that the
additive envelope
of a
\Bbbk
-linear category
\mathcal{C}
is the
additive, linear category
\mathcal{C}_{\oplus}
whose objects are formal direct sums of objects in
\mathcal{C}
and whose morphisms are
matrices of morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
, such that composition is given by matrix multiplication. The

Karoubi envelope
of an additive, linear category is a formal enhancement which results in an idempotent complete category we denote
\mathcal{C}_{\oplus,e}
.
For more information on these formal constructions, see e.g.
[
EMTW
, Sections 11.2.2 – 11.2.4]
.

3.1.1.
Soergel calculus in extended affine type A

The
diagrammatic Bott-Samelson category
of extended type
\widehat{A}_{n-1}
, denoted

\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}_{n}
, is the
\mathbb{Z}
-graded,
\mathbb{R}
-linear, pivotal category whose objects are grading shifts of finite words in the alphabet
\widehat{I}\cup\{\pm\}
, and whose vector spaces of morphisms are defined below in terms of generating diagrams and relations. We will
often identify that alphabet with the corresponding elementary Soergel bimodules
\{\mathrm{B}_{i},i\in\widehat{I}\}\cup\{\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{\pm 1}\}
, which is justified by
[
MaTh
, Theorem 2.10]
. These are bimodules over a polynomial algebra
R
, defined below (
47
). Under this identification, a word in the alphabet corresponds to a tensor product of
\mathrm{B}_{i}
and
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}
, which is called a
Bott-Samelson bimodule
. The empty word is the identity object, which is identified with
R
. The tensor product is taken over
R
, but we will often suppress
\otimes_{R}
in our notation, e.g., we will simply write
\mathrm{B}_{1}\mathrm{B}_{2}
for
\mathrm{B}_{1}\otimes_{R}\mathrm{B}_{2}
. The diagrams then correspond to
R
-
R
-bimodule maps, but we will not use those maps explicitly in this paper. As explained above, the diagrams can be seen as morphisms between degree-shifted objects or as homogeneous morphisms between unshifted objects. In this definition, we take the former point of view. As explained above, the graded version of
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}_{n}
will be denoted by
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}_{n}^{*}
.

The identity morphism on
i\in\widehat{I}
is given by a vertical non-oriented strand colored by
i
, whereas the identity morphism on
+/-
is given by a vertical upward/downward oriented black strand. As usual, we will color the unoriented strands to facilitate the reading of the diagrams. When there are too many different colors in a diagram, the colors are sometimes indicated by labels next to the strands. We say that two colors
i,j\in\widehat{I}
are
adjacent
if
i\equiv j\pm 1\bmod n
and that they are
distant
otherwise.

The number of different types of diagram increases with
n
, so below we first give
the generating diagrams for
n\geq 1
, then the additional ones for
n\geq 2
and, finally,
the additional ones that only show up for
n\geq 3
.

We read diagrams from bottom to top as morphisms, i.e., their source is at the bottom and their
target at the top.

Diagrams can be stacked vertically (composition of morphisms) and juxtaposed horizontally (monoidal product of morphisms), while adding the degrees, and are subject to the relations
below. The list contains all relations for all
n\geq 1
, but for
n=1
and
n=2
only
the relations involving the respective generators should be considered. For
n=2
, there is an additional subtlety in (
37
), as indicated.
We also assume isotopy invariance and cyclicity, meaning that closed parts of the
diagrams can be moved around freely in the plane as long as they do not cross any other strands
and the boundary is fixed, and all diagrams can be bent and rotated, and the bent and rotated
versions of the relations also hold.

Note that the empty word is the identity object in
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}_{n}
and its endomorphisms are
the closed diagrams, which by the relations above are equal to polynomials
in the colored dumbbells

As each dumbbell has degree
2
, the degree of any polynomial in these dumbbells,
as a morphism in
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
, is twice its polynomial degree. From now on,
we denote this polynomial algebra by
R
.

is central, in the sense that it can be slid through all diagrams
(i.e. it commutes horizontally with all morphisms). Note that this morphism is equal to

y
(up to sign, depending on conventions) in
[
MaTh
]
, because it is
equal to the sum of all simple roots.

Definition 3.2
.

The
extended Soergel category

\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
is the Karoubi envelope of the additive envelope of
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
.

Note that in our definition shifts are already part of
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
and recall that the idempotent complete category

\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
is Krull-Schmidt, see e.g.
[
EMTW
, Section 11.2.3]
. It therefore makes sense to consider the split Grothendieck group
[\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}]_{\oplus}
, which has a natural
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
-module structure defined by
[\mathrm{X}\langle 1\rangle]:=q[\mathrm{X}]
, for every object
\mathrm{X}\in\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
. It also has a natural algebra structure, inherited from the monoidal structure on
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
.

Finally, let us recall the
Soergel categorification theorem
, see e.g.
[
MaTh
, Theorem 2.5]
for extended affine type
A
(which was based on previous results by Härterich)
and
[
EMTW
, Theorem 11.1]
for general Coxeter type. For every
w\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
, choose a rex

\underline{w}=(s_{i_{1}},\ldots,s_{i_{l}})
and define the Bott-Samelson bimodule

\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w}):=\mathrm{B}_{i_{1}}\cdots\mathrm{B}_{i_{l}}\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}.

There is an essentially unique indecomposable summand
\mathrm{B}_{w}\in\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
of
\mathrm{BS}(\underline{w})
that is not a summand of

\mathrm{BS}(\underline{u})
for any
u\prec w
in
\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
, where
\prec
is the Bruhat order. The isomorphism class of
\mathrm{B}_{w}

does not depend on the choice of rex for
w
. More generally, for any
k\in\mathbb{Z}

and any
w\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
, the object
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{k}\mathrm{B}_{w}
is indecomposable in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
and the set of these indecomposables is complete and irredundant, meaning that they are all mutually non-isomorphic and every indecomposable in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
is isomorphic to one of them up to grading shift.
Recall further that
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
has a
q
-sesquilinear form
(-,-)
, see (
17
). Similarly,
[\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}]_{\oplus}
has a

q
-sesquilinear form
\langle-,-\rangle
, called the
graded Euler form
. To define it, one has to recall that the morphisms spaces in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext},*}_{n}

are free as left and as right graded
R
-modules and that their graded rank is finite and does not depend on whether we consider them as left or as right
R
-modules. By definition,
the value of
\langle[X],[Y]\rangle
, for
X,Y\in\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
, is equal to the graded rank of
\mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext},*}_{n}}(X,Y)
.

Theorem 3.3

(
Soergel categorification theorem).

The
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
-linear map

\displaystyle\gamma\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}\to[\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}]_{\oplus}

\displaystyle\gamma(\rho^{k}b_{w})=[\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}\mathrm{B}_{w}]\quad(k\in\mathbb{Z},w\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n})

is an isomorphism of
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
-algebras intertwining the two
q
-sesquilinear forms.

This intertwining property goes under the name of
Soergel’s hom formula

and will be used several times in Section
5.3
, so let us state it explicitly here:

(49)

(\rho^{k}b_{u},\rho^{l}b_{v})=\langle[\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}\mathrm{B}_{u}],[\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{l}}\mathrm{B}_{v}]\rangle=\underline{\mathrm{rk}}\left(\mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext},*}_{n}}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}\mathrm{B}_{u},\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{l}}\mathrm{B}_{v})\right)

for all
k,l\in\mathbb{Z}
and all
u,v\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
, where
\underline{\mathrm{rk}}
denotes the graded rank.

3.1.2.
Rouquier complexes

We give a summary of the material in
[
MMV
, §4.1]
that is needed in the sequel. In particular, we introduced a diagrammatic calculus for certain morphisms between tensor products of Rouquier complexes and Bott–Samelson bimodules in finite type
A
. In the summary
below, we recall the basic features of that calculus, generalizing it to extended affine type
A
as well. Note that it only describes part of the morphism spaces in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
, which are not yet understood in full generality. Describing the homotopy categories of Rouquier complexes in terms of generators and relations is a hard problem, even in finite type
A
, see for example
[
LiWi
]
.

Throughout the rest of the paper, if
\mathcal{C}
a
\Bbbk
-linear, additive category, for any field
\Bbbk
, we write
C^{b}(\mathcal{C})
for the category of bounded complexes in
\mathcal{C}
and
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})
for its homotopy category. If
\mathcal{C}
is also monoidal, then the usual monoidal product of chain complexes equips

K^{b}(\mathcal{C})
with a monoidal structure as well. If
\mathcal{C}
is also graded, then
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})
is bigraded
and we denote the shift inherited from
\mathcal{C}
by
\langle\cdot\rangle
and
the homological shift by
[\cdot]
.

n\geq 2

3.2.
More diagrammatic shortcuts for Rouquier complexes

We now develop some new diagrammatics to handle morphisms between tensor products of Soergel bimodules and Rouquier complexes.

For any
a,b\in\mathbb{Z}
define

\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}:=\begin{cases}\mathrm{T}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{a+1}\mathrm{T}_{a+2}\dots\mathrm{T}_{b}&\text{if $a<b$},\\[4.30554pt]
\mathrm{T}_{a}&\text{if $a=b$},\\[4.30554pt]
\mathrm{T}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{a-1}\mathrm{T}_{a-2}\dots\mathrm{T}_{b}&\text{if $a>b$},\end{cases}

where the indices on the right-hand side can be shifted modulo
n
so that they belong to
\widehat{I}=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}
. For example, we have
\mathrm{T}_{[-2,2]}=\mathrm{T}_{n-2}\mathrm{T}_{n-1}\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{1}\mathrm{T}_{2}
. Of course, the above notation is not unique, since
\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}=\mathrm{T}_{[a+kn,b+kn]}
for any
a,b,k\in\mathbb{Z}
, but we trust that this does not cause any confusion. Note that in general
\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}\neq\mathrm{T}_{[a+kn,b+ln]}
if
k\neq l
, e.g.,
\mathrm{T}_{[0,1]}=\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{1}
while
\mathrm{T}_{[n,1]}=\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{n-1}\cdots\mathrm{T}_{1}
, which are different when
n>2
. Observe that it is important that the indices
a,b
in
\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}
be integers and not residue classes modulo
n
, because that allows for products of
\mathrm{T}_{i}
whose length is greater than
n
, e.g.,
\mathrm{T}_{[0,2n-1]}=\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{1}\cdots\mathrm{T}_{n-1}\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{1}\cdots\mathrm{T}_{n-1}
.

Using the same conventions, we introduce the identity morphism on
\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}
by

\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 10.48671pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-10.48671pt\raise-4.26788pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-17.96414pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\hbox to20.97pt{\vbox to35.93pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 43.2072pt\lower-23.44714pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{
{}{{}}{}{{}}
{}{}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@setdash{0.8pt,0.5pt}{0.0pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-dasharray,stroke-dashoffset} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\color[rgb]{0,0.6,0}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}{{
{\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@setdash{0.0pt}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@roundcap\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lxSVG@roundjoin\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{}
{}{}{}

The unit and counit of the adjunction between

and its inverse are drawn as a cup and a cap, respectively, and these satisfy the usual isotopy and invertibility

).

It is useful to introduce
mergers and splitters

(60)

[a,c]
[a,b]
[b\!+\!1,c]

[a,c]
[a,b]
[b\!+\!1,c]

for
c>b\geq a
, realizing the equalities of chain complexes
\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}\mathrm{T}_{[b+1,c]}=\mathrm{T}_{[a,c]}

n>2
until the end of this section. We say that
[a,b]
and
[c,d]
are
distant
if every index appearing in
\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}
is distant from every index in
\mathrm{T}_{[c,d]}
. In this case the chain complexes
\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}\mathrm{T}_{[c,d]}^{\pm 1}
and
\mathrm{T}_{[c,d]}^{\pm 1}\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}
are isomorphic, with the isomorphism being given by
diagrams like

[a,b]

,

[e,f]

For
0<a,b<n
the chain complex
\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}B_{k}
is homotopy equivalent to

B_{k-1}\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}
when
b<k\leq a
, and homotopy equivalent to

B_{k+1}\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}
when
a\leq k<b
(note that
a\neq b
). This is proved in the same way as
[
MMV
, Lemma 4.11]
.

To prove the next lemma we will use the
hom & dot trick
. Due to its extensive use in the next section, we will briefly explain it in the following remark.

Remark 3.7

(The hom & dot trick)
.

Let
A
and
B
be two non-zero diagrams in a given morphism space.
If the latter space is one-dimensional, then
A=\lambda B
, where
\lambda
is a non-zero scalar.
To prove that
\lambda=1
we will often attach dots to certain endpoints of
A
and
B
and simplify the resulting diagrams so that they can be easily compared.

Lemma 3.8
.

For
a,b,c\in\mathbb{Z}
such that
c
is distant from
[a,b]
, the following relations hold in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
:

Proof.

We use the hom & dot trick.
By using cups and caps, both diagrams can be deformed to morphisms of degree zero from
\mathrm{B}_{c+1}
to
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}\mathrm{B}_{c}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{[a\!+\!1,b\!+\!1]}^{-1}
, which is homotopy equivalent to
\mathrm{B}_{c+1}
because

\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{[a,b]}\mathrm{B}_{c}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{[a\!+\!1,b\!+\!1]}^{-1}\simeq\mathrm{T}_{[a+1,b+1]}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{B}_{c}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{[a\!+\!1,b\!+\!1]}^{-1}\simeq\mathrm{T}_{[a+1,b+1]}\mathrm{B}_{c+1}\mathrm{T}_{[a\!+\!1,b\!+\!1]}^{-1}\simeq\mathrm{B}_{c+1}.

Soergel’s hom formula in (
49
) implies that the space of degree-preserving endomorphisms of
\mathrm{B}_{c+1}

(either in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
or in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
) is one-dimensional, so the two deformed diagrams are non-zero multiples of each other, which implies that the same holds for the two diagrams in (
74
). Attaching a dot to one of the free ends of the non-oriented strand we see that these morphisms are equal.
∎

Of course, there are other variants of (
74
) with, for example, other orientations, or involving one oriented black strand and two thick oriented strands.
Note that we can even relax the condition that
c
is distant from
[a,b]
.
We leave the details to the reader.

Until the end of this subsection, assume that
a,b\in\mathbb{Z}
such that
a<b
. By applying
[
MMV
, Lemma 4.8]
recursively, one obtains a homotopy equivalence

(75)

\mathrm{T}_{[b\!-\!1,a]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{b}\mathrm{T}_{[b\!-\!1,a]}\simeq\mathrm{T}_{[b,a\!+\!1]}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a\!+\!1]}^{-1}.

The corresponding isomorphism in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
and its inverse are represented by the diagrams

(76)

b
a
[b\!-\!1,a]
[b\!-\!1,a]
[b,a\!+\!1]
[b,a\!+\!1]

and

a
b
[b,a\!+\!1]
[b,a\!+\!1]
[b\!-\!1,a]
[b\!-\!1,a]

satisfying the relations

(77)

b
b

[b\!-\!1,\!a]
[b\!-\!1,\!a]
[b,\!a\!+\!1]
[b,\!a\!+\!1]
[b\!-\!1,\!a]

Lemma 3.10
.

We have the following in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}})
:

(82)

Proof.

We use the hom & dot trick. By using cups and caps, both diagrams are isotopic to diagrams realizing morphisms from
\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{b}\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}
to
\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}^{-1}
. Gluing the second diagram in (
76
) at the bottom results in two morphisms of degree
-1
from
\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}^{-1}
to
\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}^{-1}
.
By biadjointness and the invertibility of
\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}
in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
, there is a canonical isomorphism

\displaystyle\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}\left(\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}^{-1},\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}^{-1}\langle-1\rangle\right)

\displaystyle\cong\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{a},\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{B}_{a}\langle-1\rangle\right)

\displaystyle\cong\hom_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}}\left(\mathrm{B}_{a},\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{B}_{a}\langle-1\rangle\right)\cong\mathbb{R}.

The latter isomorphism follows from Soergel’s hom formula in (
49
) and the fact that
\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{B}_{a}\cong\mathrm{B}_{a}\langle 1\rangle\oplus\mathrm{B}_{a}\langle-1\rangle
.
By attaching dots to the free top ends labeled
a
in (
82
) and using (
80
) and (
27
), one sees that they are equal.
∎

in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}})
.

Proof.

We use the hom & dot trick again and only prove (
83
), (
84
) being similar.
As in the proof of
Lemma 3.8
, first apply cups and caps to get two degree preserving morphisms from

\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}\mathrm{B}_{c}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}^{-1}
to
\mathrm{B}_{b}\mathrm{B}_{c}
, then use the homotopy equivalences

\displaystyle\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}\mathrm{B}_{c}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}^{-1}

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}\mathrm{B}_{a}\mathrm{T}_{[b,a+1]}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{c}

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{b}\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}\mathrm{T}_{[b-1,a]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{c}

\displaystyle\simeq

\displaystyle\mathrm{B}_{b}\mathrm{B}_{c}

and the fact that
\mathrm{B}_{b}\mathrm{B}_{c}\cong\mathrm{B}_{bc}
, which implies that
\hom_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}}(\mathrm{B}_{bc},\mathrm{B}_{bc})
is one-dimensional by Soergel’s hom formula in (
49
).
We attach dots to the upper boundary points labeled
b
and
c
of the two diagrams in (
83
) and show that the resulting diagrams are equal using (
80
) and (
27
).
∎

4.
Parabolic embedding: categorified story

4.1.
The categorical embedding

Let
k,n\in\mathbb{Z}
such that
0<k<n
. In this section we are going to define a monoidal,
\mathbb{R}
-linear functor

\Psi_{k,n-k}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\boxtimes\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})

categorifying the embedding
\psi_{k,n-k}
of algebras from
Section 2.2
, but before giving the definition
in
Section 4.1.2
, we first explain the general idea behind it.

4.1.1.
Symmetric pairs of monoidal functors

The content of this subsection must be known to experts, but we do not know of any reference in the literature for what we call
a
symmetric pair of monoidal functors
in
4.2
. We thank Robert Laugwitz for pointing out to us that
our definition can be reformulated in terms of the Drinfeld centralizers of the monoidal functors, as we will briefly explain in
Remark 4.3
. Since we claim no originality in this subsection and it is only meant to help the reader understand our construction of
\Psi_{k,n-k}
, we have not endeavored to formulate the abstract notions and results in the most general setting.

As for the terminology, we call a monoidal
category or functor
strict monoidal
if the coherers of the monoidal structure are identities, otherwise we simply call it
monoidal
.
However, we should warn the reader that we treat canonical natural isomorphisms, such as the unitors and associators of
\times,\otimes

and
\oplus
, as identities. With this harmless simplification, the categories
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\boxtimes\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
and
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
are considered to be strict monoidal. However, our monoidal functor
\Psi_{k,n-k}
is definitely not strict, as will see in
Section 4.2.3
.

In this more abstract subsection, we work over an arbitrary field
\Bbbk
.
Recall that, for
\Bbbk
-linear categories
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
, their tensor product
\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D}
is the
\Bbbk
-linear category with
\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D})=\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{C})\times\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{D})
and morphism spaces
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D}}\big((\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j}),(\mathtt{k},\mathtt{l})\big)=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})\otimes\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{D}}(\mathtt{k},\mathtt{l})
, where
\otimes=\otimes_{\Bbbk}
.
Further, we define their box tensor product
\mathcal{C}\boxtimes\mathcal{D}
as the Karoubi envelope of the additive envelope of
\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D}
.

Proposition 4.1
.

Let
\mathcal{E}
be an idempotent complete additive
\Bbbk
-linear category. Then any
\Bbbk
-linear functor
\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
extends in an essentially unique way to a
\Bbbk
-linear (and hence additive) functor
\mathcal{C}_{\oplus,e}\boxtimes\mathcal{D}_{\oplus,e}\to\mathcal{E}
.

Proof.

Let
\Psi\colon\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
be a
\Bbbk
-linear functor. By the universal property of additive envelopes, this uniquely determines a functor
(\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D})_{\oplus}\to\mathcal{E}
. Since the natural inclusion
(\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D})_{\oplus}\hookrightarrow(\mathcal{C}_{\oplus}\diamond\mathcal{D}_{\oplus})_{\oplus}
is an equivalence, precomposing with an inverse equivalence yields a
\Bbbk
-linear (additive) functor
(\mathcal{C}_{\oplus}\diamond\mathcal{D}_{\oplus})_{\oplus}\to\mathcal{E}
and, since
\mathcal{E}
is idempotent complete, also a
\Bbbk
-linear (additive) functor
\Psi^{\prime}\colon(\mathcal{C}_{\oplus}\diamond\mathcal{D}_{\oplus})_{\oplus,e}\to\mathcal{E}
.

Now any pair
e_{1}
and
e_{2}
of idempotents in
\mathcal{C}_{\oplus}
and
\mathcal{D}_{\oplus}
gives rise to an idempotent
e_{1}\otimes e_{2}
in
(\mathcal{C}_{\oplus}\diamond\mathcal{D}_{\oplus})_{\oplus}
, so we obtain an embedding
\mathcal{C}_{\oplus,e}\diamond\mathcal{D}_{\oplus,e}\hookrightarrow(\mathcal{C}_{\oplus}\diamond\mathcal{D}_{\oplus})_{\oplus,e}
. Thus we can restrict our functor
\Psi^{\prime}
to a
\Bbbk
-linear functor
\mathcal{C}_{\oplus,e}\diamond\mathcal{D}_{\oplus,e}\to\mathcal{E}
.

Using the universal property of the additive envelope again, we thus obtain a
\Bbbk
-linear functor

\Psi^{\prime\prime}\colon(\mathcal{C}_{\oplus,e}\diamond\mathcal{D}_{\oplus,e})_{\oplus}\to\mathcal{E}.

Noting that
(\mathcal{C}_{\oplus,e}\diamond\mathcal{D}_{\oplus,e})_{\oplus}=\mathcal{C}_{\oplus,e}\boxtimes\mathcal{D}_{\oplus,e}
by definition, completes the proof.∎

Thus, to define
\Psi_{k,n-k}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\boxtimes\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
,
we only need to define its restriction

\Psi_{k,n-k}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\diamond\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}),

which is exactly what we will do in
Section 4.1.2
.

Suppose, additionally, that
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
have strict monoidal products
\circ_{\mathcal{C}}
and
\circ_{\mathcal{D}}
, respectively, and strict identity objects, both denoted by
\mathbbm{1}
. Then the coordinatewise monoidal product defines a strict monoidal structure on
\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D}
(taking into account
the aforementioned simplifications), and
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
can be embedded as commuting monoidal,
\Bbbk
-linear subcategories of
\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D}
by tensoring objects and morphisms on the right, resp. on the left, with
\mathbbm{1}
and
\mathrm{id}_{\mathbbm{1}}
, respectively. Another way to phrase this, is to say that the embeddings of
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
into
\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D}
form
a
commuting pair of strict monoidal,
\Bbbk
-linear functors
, although we could not find this terminology in the literature.

Suppose that
\mathcal{E}
is also strict monoidal with monoidal product
\circ_{\mathcal{E}}
and identity object
\mathbbm{1}
, and let
\Psi_{L}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{E}
and
\Psi_{R}\colon\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
be two strict monoidal,
\Bbbk
-linear functors. Then we can define the
\Bbbk
-linear functor
\Psi\colon\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
by
\Psi:=\Psi_{L}\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}
, where

(85)

\Psi(X\diamond Y):=\Psi_{L}(X)\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y)\quad\text{and}\quad\Psi(f\diamond g):=\Psi_{L}(f)\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(g),

for any objects
X\in\mathcal{C},Y\in\mathcal{D}
and any morphisms
f\in\mathcal{C},g\in\mathcal{D}
. By definition,
\Psi(X\diamond\mathbbm{1})=\Psi_{L}(X)
and

\Psi(\mathbbm{1}\diamond Y)=\Psi_{R}(Y)
for objects
X\in\mathcal{C},Y\in\mathcal{D}
, and

\Psi(f\diamond\mathrm{id}_{\mathbbm{1}})=\Psi_{L}(f)
and
\Psi(\mathrm{id}_{\mathbbm{1}}\diamond g)=\Psi_{R}(g)
for morphisms
f\in\mathcal{C},g\in\mathcal{D}
.
Of course, we could equally well define
\Psi
as
\Psi_{R}\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}
, but the latter functor need not be naturally isomorphic to
\Psi_{L}\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}
in general.

Definition 4.2
.

We say that
(\Psi_{L},\Psi_{R})
form a
symmetric pair of monoidal functors
if
there is a natural isomorphism

\zeta\colon\Psi_{L}\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}\xlongrightarrow{\cong}\Psi_{R}\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}

satisfying the
hexagon identities
, given by the commutativity of the diagrams

(86)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{L}(X_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{C}}X_{2})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{R}(Y)\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{C}}X_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{L}(X_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X_{2})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{L}(X_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y)\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{R}(Y)\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X_{2})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{(X_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{C}}X_{2})\diamond Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{\Psi_{L}(X_{1})}\,\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\,\zeta_{X_{2}\diamond Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{X_{1}\diamond Y}\,\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\,\mathrm{id}_{\Psi_{L}(X_{2})}}

and

(87)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{L}(X)\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{D}}Y_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{R}(Y_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{D}}Y_{2})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{L}(X)\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X)\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{2})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{X\diamond(Y_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{D}}Y_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{X\diamond Y_{1}}\,\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\,\mathrm{id}_{\Psi_{R}(Y_{2})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathrm{id}_{\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})}\,\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\,\zeta_{X\diamond Y_{2}}}

for all
X,X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathcal{C}
and
Y,Y_{1},Y_{2}\in\mathcal{D}
.

If we write
\Psi(X,Y):=\Psi(X\diamond Y)
and
\zeta_{X,Y}:=\zeta_{X\diamond Y}
, denote composition of morphisms in
\mathcal{E}
by
\cdot
and suppress identity morphisms, then the commutativity of the diagrams in (
86
) and (
87
) translates
to the equations

(88)

\zeta_{X_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{C}}X_{2},Y}=\zeta_{X_{1},Y}\cdot\zeta_{X_{2},Y}\quad\text{and}\quad\zeta_{X,Y_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{D}}Y_{2}}=\zeta_{X,Y_{2}}\cdot\zeta_{X,Y_{1}},

respectively. These are very similar to the hexagon identities for a braiding, which is symmetric because
\zeta_{X,Y}^{-1}
defines the braiding for
(\Psi_{R},\Psi_{L})
. This justifies our choice of terminology in
4.2
. Note that the commutative diagrams
in (
86
) and (
87
) are actually pentagons in our case,
because we have omitted the sixth side of the usual hexagons, which in our case is an identity,
due to our assumption that the underlying monoidal categories are strict. In fact,
those pentagons could be reduced to triangles, since two of the remaining five sides are also identities, but we have decided to include them for clarity.

Note that the embeddings of
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
into
\mathcal{C}\diamond\mathcal{D}
form a symmetric pair of monoidal,
\Bbbk
-linear functors with trivial braiding, in the sense that there is an equality
\Psi_{L}(X)\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y)=\Psi_{R}(Y)\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X)
and
\zeta_{X,Y}=\mathrm{id}_{\Psi(X,Y)}
for all objects
X\in\mathcal{C},Y\in\mathcal{D}
.

Before we go on, let us explain the aforementioned relation with Drinfeld centralizers.

Remark 4.3
.

Let
\mathcal{A}
and
\mathcal{B}
be two strict monoidal,
\Bbbk
-linear categories and
F\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{B}
a strict monoidal,
\Bbbk
-linear functor between
them. The
Drinfeld centralizer of
F
, denoted
\mathcal{Z}_{F}=\mathcal{Z}_{F}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{B})
, is the
\Bbbk
-linear category whose objects
are pairs
(B,\beta)
, with
B\in\mathcal{B}
an object and

\beta\colon F(-)\circ_{\mathcal{B}}B\xrightarrow{\cong}B\circ_{\mathcal{B}}F(-)

a natural isomorphism (called
half-braiding
) satisfying
\beta_{A_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{A}}A_{2}}=\beta_{A_{1}}\cdot\beta_{A_{2}}
for

A_{1},A_{2}\in\mathcal{A}
(where we are suppressing two identity morphisms, as before). The morphisms in
\mathcal{Z}_{F}
are morphisms in
\mathcal{B}

which commute with the respective
\beta
’s. The category
\mathcal{Z}_{F}
has an obvious monoidal structure such that the
forgetful functor
\mathrm{Forget}:\mathcal{Z}_{F}\to\mathcal{B}
, defined by
(B,\beta)\mapsto B
, is a monoidal functor.
For more information on Drinfeld centralizers, see
e.g.
[
Hoe
, Section 1.5]
(especially Example 1.5.3) and
[
ElHo
, Section 2.8]
and references therein. Note that Hoek uses the term
Drinfeld center
, whereas Elias and Hogancamp use the term
Drinfeld centralizer
, which we find more adequate and therefore adopt here as well.

If
(\Psi_{L},\Psi_{R},\zeta)
is a symmetric pair of strict monoidal functors, then
\Psi_{L}
and
\Psi_{R}
factor through each other’s Drinfeld centralizers, i.e., both diagrams below commute.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}

In general, a pair of monoidal functors
F\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{E}
and
G\colon\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{E}
which factor through each other’s Drinfeld centralizers only yields two half-braidings.
The factorization of
F
through
\mathcal{Z}_{G}
yields isomorphisms
\beta_{X,Y}
, which satisfy the hexagon identity w.r.t.
X\in\mathcal{C}
, and the factorization of
G
through
\mathcal{Z}_{F}
yields isomorphisms
\beta_{Y,X}
, which satisfy the hexagon identity w.r.t.
Y\in\mathcal{D}
.
However, two half-braidings do not necessarily add up to one braiding, which has to satisfy the hexagon identities for both variables
at once. In our case they do add up to a braiding, because they satisfy the additional condition
\beta_{Y,X}=\beta_{X,Y}^{-1}
.

Lemma 4.4
.

The functor
\Psi
in (
85
) extends to a monoidal functor, which restricts to the strict monoidal functors
\Psi_{L}
and
\Psi_{R}
,
if and only if
\Psi_{L},\Psi_{R}
form a symmetric pair of monoidal functors.

Proof.

Suppose that
\Psi
extends to a monoidal functor. Then there exists a natural isomorphism

(89)

\Psi(X_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{C}}X_{2},Y_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{D}}Y_{2})\xlongrightarrow{\eta_{(X_{1},Y_{1}),(X_{2},Y_{2})}}\Psi(X_{1},Y_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi(X_{2},Y_{2})

for any objects
X_{1},X_{2}\in\mathcal{C}
and
Y_{1},Y_{2}\in\mathcal{D}
. Note that

\Psi(\mathbbm{1},\mathbbm{1})=\Psi_{L}(\mathbbm{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(\mathbbm{1})=\mathbbm{1}\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\mathbbm{1}=\mathbbm{1}
holds on the nose, so
\eta
is the only coherer that
can be non-trivial.

By definition, the object on the l.h.s. of (
89
) is equal to

(90)

\Psi_{L}(X_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X_{2})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{2})

while the object on the r.h.s. is equal to

(91)

\Psi_{L}(X_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X_{2})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{2}),

hence
\eta_{(X_{1},Y_{1}),(X_{2},Y_{2})}
in (
89
) is completely determined by the natural isomorphism

(92)

\Psi_{L}(X_{2})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\xrightarrow{\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{1}}}\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}(X_{2}),

where
\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{1}}:=\eta_{(\mathbbm{1},Y_{1}),(X_{2},\mathbbm{1})}
. Note that we have swapped the order of
X_{2}
and
Y_{1}
in the subscript of
\zeta
,
which conforms to the notation of a braiding.

Let
X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}\in\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and
Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3}\in\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
. The usual coherence condition for
\eta
is

(93)

\eta_{(X_{2},Y_{2}),(X_{3},Y_{3})}\cdot\eta_{(X_{1},Y_{1}),(X_{2}\circ_{\mathcal{C}}X_{3},Y_{2}\circ_{\mathcal{D}}Y_{3})}=\eta_{(X_{1},Y_{1}),(X_{2},Y_{2})}\cdot\eta_{(X_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{C}}X_{2},Y_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{D}}Y_{2}),(X_{2},Y_{3})},

where we have suppressed several identity morphisms again. By the
same arguments as above, we obtain the corresponding coherence condition for
\zeta
:

(94)

\zeta_{X_{3},Y_{2}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{2}\circ_{\mathcal{C}}X_{3},Y_{1}}=\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{1}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{3},Y_{1}\circ_{\mathcal{D}}Y_{2}}.

Note that the coherence conditions in (
93
) and (
94
) are equivalent.

The hexagon identities for
\zeta
are obtained from (
94
) as special cases, by putting
Y_{2}=\mathbbm{1}
and
X_{2}=\mathbbm{1}
, respectively. This proves that
\Psi_{L},\Psi_{R}
is a symmetric pair of monoidal functors.

Conversely, suppose that
\Psi_{L},\Psi_{R}
is a symmetric pair of monoidal functors with braiding
\zeta
. Thanks to the interchange law for morphisms in a monoidal category, we have

(95)

\zeta_{X_{3},Y_{2}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{1}}=\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{1}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{3},Y_{2}},

as can be seen from the corresponding commutative diagram:

(96)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{L}(X_{2})\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\Psi_{L}(X_{3})\Psi_{R}(Y_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\Psi_{L}(X_{2})\Psi_{L}(X_{3})\Psi_{R}(Y_{2})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{L}(X_{2})\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\Psi_{R}(Y_{2})\Psi_{L}(X_{3})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{R}(Y_{1})\Psi_{L}(X_{2})\Psi_{R}(Y_{2})\Psi_{L}(X_{3})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{X_{3},Y_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{X_{3},Y_{2}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{1}}}

Multiplying both sides in (
95
) on the right by
\zeta_{X_{3},Y_{1}}
and using the hexagon identities yields (
94
), which implies that
\eta
satisfies (
93
). This proves that
\Psi
extends to a monoidal functor.
∎

The following corollary shows that our choice to define
\Psi
as
\Psi_{L}\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}
, instead of
\Psi_{R}\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}
, is not
essential if the pair of monoidal functors
\Psi_{L},\Psi_{R}
is symmetric. The proof uses similar arguments
as the proof of
Lemma 4.4
and is straightforward, so we leave the details to the reader.

Corollary 4.5
.

Suppose that
\Psi_{L},\Psi_{R}
is a symmetric pair of monoidal functors. Then
\Psi_{L}\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{R}

and
\Psi_{R}\circ_{\mathcal{E}}\Psi_{L}
are two naturally isomorphic monoidal functors.

Remark 4.6
.

The functor
\Psi
in
Lemma 4.4
is a strict monoidal functor if and only if the braiding
\zeta
is trivial.

4.1.2.
Definition of
\Psi_{k,n-k}
and main theorem

As in
Section 4.1.1
, we first define two strict monoidal
\Bbbk
-linear functors

\Psi_{L}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})\quad\text{and}\quad\Psi_{R}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})

and then define

(97)

\Psi_{k,n-k}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\diamond\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})

by

\Psi_{k,n-k}(X\diamond Y):=\Psi_{L}(X)\Psi_{R}(Y)\quad\text{and}\quad\Psi_{k,n-k}(f\diamond g)=\Psi_{L}(f)\Psi_{R}(g),

for any objects
X\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k},Y\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
and any morphisms
f\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k},g\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
. We have omitted the symbol
for the monoidal product in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
. To avoid cluttering in certain diagrams of the definition below, we have reduced the number of labels. When there are several strands of the same color, we often label just one of them. The labels of the others are understood to be the same.

On objects

On the generating objects,
\Psi_{L}
and
\Psi_{R}
are defined by

\displaystyle\Psi_{L}\colon\begin{cases}\mathrm{B}_{i}\mapsto\mathrm{B}_{i},\quad i=1,\dotsc,k-1,\\
\mathrm{B}_{0}\mapsto\mathrm{T}_{k}^{-1}\dotsm\mathrm{T}_{n-1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{n-1}\dotsm\mathrm{T}_{k},\\
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mapsto\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{n-1}\dots\mathrm{T}_{k},\\
\end{cases}

\displaystyle\Psi_{R}\colon\begin{cases}\mathrm{B}_{j}\mapsto\mathrm{B}_{k+j},\quad j=1,\dotsc,n-k-1,\\
\mathrm{B}_{0}\mapsto T_{0}\dotsm\mathrm{T}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{k-1}^{-1}\dotsm\mathrm{T}_{0}^{-1},\\
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mapsto\mathrm{T}_{k}^{-1}\dots\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}.\end{cases}

On morphisms

•

If
D_{1,\dotsc,k-1}
is a morphism of
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
in colors
(1,\dotsc,k-1)
, then

\Psi_{L}(D_{1,\dotsc,k-1}):=D_{1,\dotsc,k-1},

•

If
D^{\prime}_{1,\dotsc,k-1}
is a morphism of
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
in colors
(1,\dotsc,n-k-1)
, then

\Psi_{R}(D^{\prime}_{1,\dotsc,n-k-1}):=D^{\prime}_{k+1,\dotsc,n-1},

On other morphisms,
\Psi_{L}
and
\Psi_{R}
are defined as follows.

.

The inner labels in the last line are
{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}n-1}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.38,0.43,0.77}[n-2,k-1]}
(left) and
{\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}k-1}
and
{\color[rgb]{0.06,0.46,1}[-1,k-2]}
(right). This ends the definition of
\Psi_{L}
and
\Psi_{R}
.

Lemma 4.7
.

For any domain
X
and codomain
Y
of a generating morphism in
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
of degree
t
, we have

\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\Psi_{L}(X),\Psi_{L}(Y)\langle t\rangle)\cong\hom_{\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}}(X,Y\langle t\rangle).

Similarly, for any domain
Z
and codomain
W
of a generating morphism in
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
of degree
t
, we have

\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\Psi_{R}(Z),\Psi_{R}(W)\langle t\rangle)\cong\hom_{\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}}(Z,W\langle t\rangle).

Moreover, all those morphism spaces are one-dimensional.

Proof.

The proof is immediate except for two cases in
\Psi_{L}
and two cases in
\Psi_{R}
:

•

a crossing in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
involving an oriented strand and unoriented strands labeled
0
and
k-1
, respectively in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
with labels
0
and
n-k-1
;

•

a six-valent vertex in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
involving strands labeled
0
and
k-1
, respectively in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
with labels
0
and
n-k-1
.

We only prove the second part of each case, the first being similar.

For a crossing in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
involving an oriented strand and unoriented strands labeled
0
and
n-k-1
we compute

\displaystyle\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\Psi_{R}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{B}_{n-k-1}),\Psi_{R}(\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}))\mspace{-220mu}

\displaystyle\cong\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\mathrm{T}_{[1,k]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{B}_{n-1},\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{[1,k]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho})

\displaystyle\cong\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\mathrm{T}_{[1,k]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{0},\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{[1,k]}^{-1})

\displaystyle\cong\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\mathrm{B}_{0},\mathrm{T}_{[1,k]}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{[1,k]}^{-1})

\displaystyle\mspace{-4mu}\overset{\eqref{eq:homotopeq2}}{\cong}\!\!\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\mathrm{B}_{0},\mathrm{B}_{0})\cong\hom_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}}(\mathrm{B}_{0},\mathrm{B}_{0})\cong\hom_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}}(\mathrm{B}_{0},\mathrm{B}_{0})

\displaystyle\cong\hom_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{B}_{n-k-1},\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}).

For a six-valent vertex in
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
involving strands labeled
0
and
n-k-1
we compute

\displaystyle\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\Psi_{R}(\mathrm{B}_{n-k-1}\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{B}_{n-k-1}),\Psi_{R}(\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{B}_{n-k-1}\mathrm{B}_{0}))\mspace{-460mu}

\displaystyle\cong\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\mathrm{B}_{n-1}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{n-1},\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{n-1}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}^{-1})

\displaystyle\cong\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{n-1}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{n-1}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{n-1}\mathrm{T}_{[0,k-1]}\mathrm{B}_{k},\mathbbm{1})

\displaystyle\mspace{-4mu}\overset{\eqref{eq:homotopeq2}}{\cong}\!\!\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\mathrm{T}_{[-1,k-2]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\!\mathrm{T}_{[-1,k-2]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[-1,k-2]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\!\mathrm{T}_{[-1,k-2]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[-1,k-2]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\!\mathrm{T}_{[-1,k-2]}\mathrm{B}_{k},\!\mathbbm{1})

\displaystyle\cong\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k},\!\mathbbm{1})\cong\hom_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}}(\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1},\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k})

\displaystyle\cong\hom_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}}(\mathrm{B}_{n-k-1}\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{B}_{n-k-1},\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{B}_{n-k-1}\mathrm{B}_{0}).\qed

4.2.
Proof of the main theorem

Lemma 4.8
.

The
\mathbb{R}
-linear, strict monoidal functors
\Psi_{L}
and
\Psi_{R}
from
Section 4.1.2

(1)

are well-defined;

(2)

form a symmetric pair.

Theorem 4.9
.

The symmetric pair
\Psi_{L},\Psi_{R}
gives rise to an
\mathbb{R}
-linear, monoidal functor

\Psi_{k,n-k}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\boxtimes\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}).

Proof.

By
Lemma 4.4
and
Lemma 4.8
, the
\mathbb{R}
-linear functor in (
97
)

\Psi_{k,n-k}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\diamond\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})

extends to a monoidal functor, which in turn gives rise to an

\mathbb{R}
-linear, monoidal functor

\Psi_{k,n-k}\colon\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\boxtimes\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}),

as explained in
Section 4.1.1
.
∎

It remains to prove
Lemma 4.8
, which will be done in
Section 4.2.1
and
Section 4.2.3
.

4.2.1.
Well-definedness

The proofs that
\Psi_{L}
and
\Psi_{R}
preserve all diagrammatic relations are very similar, so
we only prove that
\Psi_{L}
is well-defined. Because of the two cases in (
37
), the proof that
\Psi_{L}
is well-defined contains four cases:
1=k=n-1
,
1=k<n-1
,

2=k<n
and
2<k<n
. However, the first two cases are proved in the same way as the corresponding part in the fourth case. The third case is also almost the same as the corresponding part of the fourth case, except for the proof that
\Psi_{L}
preserves (
37
), which we therefore prove separately at the end of this subsection.

Suppose that
k>2
. Since
\Psi_{L}
is the identity on diagrams only involving colors different from
0
and
k-1
it preserves the relations involving only those diagrams.

(a1)

Relations (
26
) to (
29
) for
i=0
follow by isotopy and similar arguments as in the first bullet point in the proof of
[
MMV
, Theorem 5.4]
.

(a2)

Relations (
30
) to (
33
) for
i=0
or
k=0
are verified using the relations in (
68
) and the usual Soergel calculus.

(a3)

Relations (
34
) to (
37
) for
\{i,j\}=\{0,1\}
are checked using similar arguments as in the third bullet point in the proof of
[
MMV
, Theorem 5.4]
.

(a4)

Relations (
34
) to (
37
) for
\{i,j\}=\{0,k-1\}
are more involved and we give a sample computation for relation (
35
), with the proof of the other relations being similar.
We have

(a7)

) are

define morphisms in

\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}\left(\mathrm{T}_{[n-1,k]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{[n\!-\!1,k]}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{T}_{[n-1,k]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{[n-1,k]},\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{[n-1,k]}\mathrm{B}_{k-2}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k-2}\mathrm{T}_{[n-1,k]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{-1}\right).

This morphism space is one-dimensional, as can be seen as follows. By (
75
) (with
a=k
and
b=0
) and (
68
), we have
\mathrm{T}_{[n-1,k]}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{[n\!-\!1,k]}\simeq\mathrm{T}_{[n,k+1]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[n,k+1]}^{-1}
and
\mathrm{T}_{[n,k+1]}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\simeq\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{T}_{[n,k+1]}
.
This implies that the domain is homotopy equivalent to

\mathrm{T}_{[n,k+1]}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{T}_{[n,k+1]}^{-1}
. Commuting
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}
with all factors from left to right shows that the codomain is homotopy equivalent to
\mathrm{T}_{[n,k+1]}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{T}_{[n,k+1]}^{-1}
. By adjunction, the above morphism space is therefore
isomorphic to
\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k},\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\right)
. Moreover, we have

\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k},\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\right)\cong\mathrm{hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}}\left(\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k},\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\mathrm{B}_{k}\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\right)

and the latter morphism space is one-dimensional (thanks to Soergel’s hom formula in (
49
)).

We attach a dot to the free end at the top labeled
\color[rgb]{1,0.5,0}k-1
of the diagrams at the right-hand sides of (
98
).
For the left diagram in (
98
), use (
34
) to get rid of the 6-valent vertex and obtain two terms which can be further simplified by relations (
80
), (
45
) and (
63
). For the right diagram in (
98
), first use (
80
), (
45
) and (
68
) to slide the dot closer to the 6-valent vertex, then proceed as in the previous case. In the end, we see that both diagrams in (

k=2
. As already mentioned, it only remains to check (
37
) in this case. We have

∎

4.2.2.
Definition of
\zeta

We will first show that for every pair of objects
X\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k},Y\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
, there is an isomorphism in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})

\zeta_{X,Y}\colon\Psi_{L}(X)\Psi_{R}(Y)\xlongrightarrow{\cong}\Psi_{R}(Y)\Psi_{L}(X)

and that these isomorphisms satisfy the hexagon identities from
4.2
.
After that, we will show that
\zeta
is natural in
X
and
Y
.

We define
\zeta_{X,Y}
for pairs of generating objects
X\in\{\mathrm{B}_{i},\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\}\subset\mathrm{Ob}(\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k})
and

Y\in\{\mathrm{B}_{i},\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\}\subset\mathrm{Ob}(\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k})
and extend the
definition recursively to pairs of monoidal products of generating objects (corresponding to Bott-Samelson bimodules) by
the hexagon identities. Concretely, we put

(99)

\zeta_{X_{1}X_{2},Y_{1}Y_{2}}:=\zeta_{X_{1},Y_{1}Y_{2}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{1}Y_{2}}=\zeta_{X_{1},Y_{2}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{1},Y_{1}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{2}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{1}}

for any objects
X_{1},X_{2}\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and
Y_{1},Y_{2}\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
. Alternatively, we could have put

(100)

\zeta_{X_{1}X_{2},Y_{1}Y_{2}}:=\zeta_{X_{1}X_{2},Y_{2}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{1}X_{2},Y_{1}}=\zeta_{X_{1},Y_{2}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{2}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{1},Y_{1}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{1}},

but the expressions in (
99
) and (
100
) are equal because
\zeta_{X_{1},Y_{1}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{2}}=\zeta_{X_{2},Y_{2}}\cdot\zeta_{X_{1},Y_{1}}
thanks to the interchange law, see (
95
). In particular,
the isomorphisms
\zeta_{X,Y}
satisfy the hexagon identities by definition.

After this explanation, it remains to define
\zeta_{X,Y}
for pairs of generating objects.

In all cases below,
\zeta_{X,Y}
is obtained by composing invertible morphisms in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
. To see this, one notes that all diagrams appearing are isotopic to a diagram where at each height there is either a trivalent vertex, a four-valent vertex (a crossing), a six-valent one (all involving at least one oriented strand), or just vertical strands. One checks easily that all of them are invertible (this is implied by the various relations in
Section 3.1
and
Section 3.2
), hence so is their composite. Therefore, we only give the diagrams for
\zeta_{X,Y}
without further explanation.
