In

\zeta_{\mathrm{B}_{\rho},\mathrm{B}_{0}}
,
\color[rgb]{1,0.47,0.62}\mathrm{T}_{[-1,k\!-\!2]}=\mathrm{T}_{n-1}\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{1}\dotsm\mathrm{T}_{k-2}
,
and in

\zeta_{\mathrm{B}_{0},\mathrm{B}_{0}}
,
\color[rgb]{1,0.04,0.61}a=[1,k\!-\!2]
and
\color[rgb]{0,1,1}b=[n\!-\!2,k\!+\!1]
.

This completes the definition of
\zeta
.

4.2.3.
Naturality of
\zeta

To show that
\zeta
is natural, we have to prove commutativity of the diagram

(101)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{L}(X)\Psi_{R}(Y)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{R}(Y)\Psi_{L}(X)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{L}(W)\Psi_{R}(Z)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{R}(Z)\Psi_{L}(W)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{L}(f)\Psi_{R}(g)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{X,Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Psi_{R}(g)\Psi_{L}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\zeta_{W,Z}}

for all objects
X,W\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and
Y,Z\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
, and all morphisms

f\in\mathrm{hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}}(X,W)
and
g\in\mathrm{hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}}(Y,Z)
. Thanks to the hexagon identities for
\zeta
and
the interchange law for morphisms in
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
, it suffices to show commutativity in (
101
) for pairs

(f,g)
where
f
is a generating morphism in
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and
g=\mathrm{id}_{Y}
for some generating object
Y\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
,
or
f=\mathrm{id}_{X}
for some generating object
X\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and
g
is a generating morphism in
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
.
Finally, we note that the proof for pairs of the first type and the proof for pairs of the second type are very similar, so we only give the proof for pairs of the second type below.
Concretely, those pairs are
(\mathrm{id}_{X},g)
, where
X\in\{\mathrm{B}_{\rho},\mathrm{B}_{0},\ldots,\mathrm{B}_{k-1}\}
and
g
is one of the generators in (
23
), (
24
) or (
25
) with labels in
\{\rho,0,\ldots,n-k-1\}
. The only cases
in which commutativity of (
101
) is not immediate, is when
X\in\{\mathrm{B}_{\rho},\mathrm{B}_{0}\}
and/or the labels of some strands of
g
belong to
\{0,\rho\}
.

Note that checking commutativity of (
101
) always consists of verifying the equality of two diagrams, both belonging to the same morphism space.
In all but two cases the dimension of the morphism space in the given degree is one-dimensional (see
Lemma 4.11
), so we can use the hom & dot trick, explained in
Remark 3.7
. The remaining two cases are checked directly.

Lemma 4.11
.

For each generating object
X
of
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}
and each generating morphism
g\colon Y\to Z
in
\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}
, there are objects
U,V\in\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
and an isomorphism

(102)

\hom_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\Psi_{L}(X)\Psi_{R}(Y),\Psi_{R}(Z)\Psi_{L}(X))\cong\hom_{\widehat{\mathcal{BS}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}}(U,V).

Unless
X=\mathrm{B}_{0}
and
g\colon 1\to\mathrm{B}_{0}
is a dot labeled 0 or
g\colon\mathrm{B}_{0}\to\mathrm{B}_{0}\mathrm{B}_{0}
is a trivalent vertex labeled 0, the two morphism spaces in
(
102
)
are one-dimensional by Soergel’s hom formula in (
49
).

Proof.

We first note that by invertibility of
\zeta_{X,Y}
we have
\Psi_{R}(W)\Psi_{L}(X)\cong\Psi_{L}(X)\Psi_{R}(W)
and we need to compute
\mathrm{Hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})}(\Psi_{L}(X)\Psi_{R}(Z),\Psi_{L}(X)\Psi_{R}(W))
.
For invertible
X
, the claim follows from
Lemma 4.7
and therefore we have to consider only the cases
X=\mathrm{B}_{i}
.
The case of
i>0
is an easy computation in the lines of the proof of
Lemma 4.7
. For
i=0
we proceed case-by-case.

We use the hom & dot trick. At the top of both diagrams we attach a dot at the endpoints labeled
\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}0
and
\color[rgb]{0.21,0.12,1}k
. At the bottom we attach dots to the endpoints labeled
\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}0
,
\color[rgb]{0.21,0.12,1}k
and the leftmost endpoint labeled
{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k+1}
.

On the resulting diagram at the left-hand side, we use (
106
) twice and (
104
) to pull all dots to the bottom. Using (
59
) and (
68
) we obtain

(119)

[0,k\!-\!1]
k\!+\!1
k+1
[n\!-\!1,k]
0

On the right-hand side, we use (a variant of) (
104
) to pull the dots labeled
\color[rgb]{0.5,0,0.5}0
close to the box
\zeta_{\mathrm{B}_{0},\mathrm{B}_{0}}
and use (
59
) to obtain

(120)

[0,k\!-\!1]
k+1
[n\!-\!1,k]
\zeta_{\mathrm{B}_{0},\mathrm{B}_{0}}
k

Finally, applying (
106
) to slide the dot labeled
\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}k
up through the box, using (
68
) to slide the dot labeled
\color[rgb]{0,0,1}k\!+\!1
through the strand labeled
\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}[0,k\!-\!1]
, and using (
59
) on the strands labeled
\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}[0,k\!-\!1]
with endpoints at the bottom gives (
119
).

This ends the proof of the naturality of
\zeta
. ∎

.

Conjecture 4.15
.

The functor
\Psi_{k,n-k}
descends to a faithful functor

\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{k}\boxtimes_{y}\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n-k}\to K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
.

5.
Parabolic induction: an example

5.1.
The decategorified story

In this section, we will work out an explicit example of an induced triangulated birepresentation
\mathbf{W}
of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
and its wide finitary cover
\mathbf{U}
. Below, we will start with the decategorified story, before we move on to the categorification, after a general intermezzo on completions of additive categories. The categorified story is divided into two parts: one dedicated to
\mathbf{U}
and another to
\mathbf{W}
. Both birepresentations are defined using a certain algebra object
\mathrm{Y}
in a completion of
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})
, but the construction of
\mathbf{W}
is much less straightforward than that of
\mathbf{U}
, as the reader will see.

5.1.1.
The Hecke algebra
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}

Recall that
\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{2}
is generated by two simple reflections
s_{0}
and
s_{1}
which are only subject to the quadratic relations

s_{0}^{2}=e=s_{1}^{2}
. Any element in
\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{2}
has therefore a unique rex, which can be identified with an alternating binary sequence.
To work with those, we have to introduce some notation. For
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
and
i\in\{0,1\}
, let
\widehat{m}_{\,i}
and
{}_{i}\widehat{m}
denote the alternating binary sequences of length
m
ending with
i
and starting with
i
, respectively. If
\widehat{m}_{\,j}={}_{i}\widehat{m}
for certain
m\in\mathbb{Z}
and
i,j\in\{0,1\}
(we call this a
parity condition
), then we write
{}_{i}\widehat{m}_{\,j}
for that
alternating sequence to make the computations below easier to read. For example,

\widehat{4}_{\,0}={}_{1}\widehat{4}={}_{1}\widehat{4}_{\,0}=1010
. By convention, we put
\widehat{0}_{\,i}={}_{i}\widehat{0}=\emptyset
, for
i\in\{0,1\}
,
which of course corresponds to the neutral element
e\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{2}
.

The extended affine symmetric group
\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{2}^{\mathrm{ext}}
has an extra generator
\rho
of infinite order, and two extra relations:
\rho s_{0}\rho^{-1}=s_{1}
and
\rho s_{1}\rho^{-1}=s_{0}
.

The extended affine Hecke algebra
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
is generated by
T_{0},T_{1}
and
\rho^{\pm 1}
, subject to only the first relation in (
8
) and all relations in (
9
).
In this case, it is easy to express the KL basis elements
b_{w}
in terms of the regular basis elements
T_{u}
explicitly:

(121)

b_{w}=\sum_{u\preceq w}q^{\ell(w)-\ell(u)}T_{u},

where
\preceq
denotes the Bruhat order on
\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{2}
. Note that
u\preceq w
holds iff the rex for
u
is an alternating binary subsequence of the rex for
w
and it is easy to invert this change of basis:

(122)

T_{w}=\sum_{u\preceq w}(-q)^{\ell(w)-\ell(u)}b_{u}.

The multiplication constants w.r.t. the KL basis are also easy to compute in this case and are all equal to 0, 1, 2 or
[2]=q+q^{-1}
. For
m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}
(assuming that the parity conditions are met in each line below), we have

(123)

\begin{gathered}b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}b_{{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}=[2]\left(b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-1}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-3}_{\,1}}+\ldots+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+3}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+1}_{\,1}}\right);\\
b_{{}_{0}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}b_{{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}=[2]\left(b_{{}_{0}\widehat{m+n-1}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{0}\widehat{m+n-3}_{\,1}}+\ldots+b_{{}_{0}\widehat{|m-n|+3}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{0}\widehat{|m-n|+1}_{\,1}}\right);\\
b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}b_{{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,0}}=[2]\left(b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-1}_{\,0}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-3}_{\,0}}+\ldots+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+3}_{\,0}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+1}_{\,0}}\right);\\
b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,0}}b_{{}_{0}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}=[2]\left(b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-1}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-3}_{\,1}}+\ldots+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+3}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+1}_{\,1}}\right);\\
b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}b_{{}_{0}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}=b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n}_{\,1}}+2b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-2}_{\,1}}+\ldots+2b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+2}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|}_{\,1}};\\
b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,0}}b_{{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}=b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n}_{\,1}}+2b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-2}_{\,1}}+\ldots+2b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+2}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|}_{\,1}};\\
b_{{}_{0}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}b_{{}_{0}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}=\begin{cases}b_{{}_{0}\widehat{2m}_{\,1}}+2b_{{}_{0}\widehat{2m-2}_{\,1}}+\ldots+2b_{{}_{0}\widehat{2}_{\,1}},&\text{if}\;m=n\\
b_{{}_{0}\widehat{m+n}_{\,1}}+2b_{{}_{0}\widehat{m+n-2}_{\,1}}+\ldots+2b_{{}_{0}\widehat{|m-n|+2}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{0}\widehat{|m-n|}_{\,1}},&\text{if}\;m\neq n\end{cases};\\
b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}b_{{}_{0}\widehat{n}_{\,0}}=\begin{cases}b_{{}_{1}\widehat{2m}_{\,0}}+2b_{{}_{1}\widehat{2m-2}_{\,0}}+\ldots+2b_{{}_{1}\widehat{2}_{\,0}},&\text{if}\;m=n\\
b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n}_{\,0}}+2b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-2}_{\,0}}+\ldots+2b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+2}_{\,0}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|}_{\,0}},&\text{if}\;m\neq n\end{cases};\end{gathered}

and the analogous equations with
0
and
1
swapped. These formulas are certainly known to experts, but we couldn’t find an explicit reference for all of them in the literature (the first formula can be found in
[
Lus
, Proposition 7.7(a)]
). Let us, therefore, briefly explain how we obtained them. There is a close relation between

\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
and a two-colored version of the Grothendieck ring of finite-dimensional representations (of type I) of quantum
\mathfrak{sl}_{2}
,
see
[
Eli1
, Section 2.2.1]
. In the first four cases above, when the last element of the left alternating binary sequence and
the first element of the right alternating binary sequence are equal, this correspondence is given by the bijection

b_{{}_{i}\widehat{m}_{\,j}}\longleftrightarrow[2][V_{m-1}],

where
[V_{m-1}]
is the Grothendieck class of the (essentially unique)
m
-dimensional irreducible representation of quantum
\mathfrak{sl}_{2}
. Note that
the Grothendieck ring over
\mathbb{Z}
must be tensored with
\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
for multiplication by
[2]
to make sense. In the first case, for example, we get

\displaystyle b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}b_{{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}\longleftrightarrow

\displaystyle[2]^{2}[V_{m-1}][V_{n-1}]=

\displaystyle[2]^{2}\left([V_{m+n-2}]+[V_{m+n-4}]+\ldots+[V_{|m-n|+2}]+[V_{|m-n|}]\right)\longleftrightarrow

\displaystyle[2]\left(b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-1}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m+n-3}_{\,1}}+\ldots+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+3}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{|m-n|+1}_{\,1}}\right),

where we have used the well-known Clebsch-Gordan rule for the decomposition of the tensor product of two finite dimensional irreducible representations of quantum
\mathfrak{sl}_{2}
. It is well-known that
b_{i}b_{{}_{i}\widehat{m}_{\,j}}=b_{{}_{i}\widehat{m}_{\,j}}b_{j}=[2]b_{{}_{i}\widehat{m}_{\,j}}
, for
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}
and
i,j\in\{0,1\}
satisfying the parity condition. The remaining cases above can be reduced to the first four cases (sometimes with
0
and
1
swapped) by that basic multiplication rule and a simple trick, assuming (just for the sake of this trick) that we work over

\mathbb{Q}(q)
for example. Suffice it to give an illustrative example:

b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}b_{{}_{0}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}=\frac{1}{[2]}(b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}b_{1})b_{{}_{0}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}=\frac{1}{[2]}b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}(b_{1}b_{{}_{0}\widehat{n}_{\,1}})=\frac{1}{[2]}b_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}_{\,1}}(b_{{}_{1}\widehat{n+1}_{\,1}}+b_{{}_{1}\widehat{n-1}_{\,1}}).

Recall the standard trace
\epsilon\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}\to\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]
from (
16
) and
the associated
q
-sesquilinear form
(-,-)
on
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
from (
17
). The formula in (
121
) implies that

\epsilon(b_{w})=q^{\ell(w)}

for any
w\in\widehat{\mathfrak{S}}_{n}
. Note further that
\omega(b_{{}_{i}\widehat{m}_{\,j}})=b_{{}_{j}\widehat{m}_{\,i}}
, for
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
and
i,j\in\{0,1\}
. The following lemma, which is an immediate consequence of the above, is a more detailed version of
2.2
in
this particular case and will be needed in
Section 5.3
.

Lemma 5.1
.

For any
r,s\in\mathbb{Z}
and
i,j,k,l\in\{0,1\}
, we have
(\rho^{r}b_{{}_{i}\widehat{m}_{\,j}},\rho^{s}b_{{}_{k}\widehat{n}_{\,l}})=\delta_{r,s}(b_{{}_{i}\widehat{m}_{\,j}},b_{{}_{k}\widehat{n}_{\,l}})
and

(b_{{}_{i}\widehat{m}_{\,j}},b_{{}_{k}\widehat{n}_{\,l}})=\begin{cases}q^{2}p(q),&\text{if}\;\,m=n\;\wedge\;i\neq k\;\wedge\;j\neq l;\\
q^{|m-n|}p^{\prime}(q)&\text{else},\end{cases}

where
p(q),p^{\prime}(q)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}[q]
have constant terms equal to two and to one, respectively.

5.1.2.
Two representations of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}

Let
V=\mathrm{Span}\{v\}
be the trivial one-dimensional
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{1}
-module, defined by

\rho(v)=v,

and let

W:=V\odot V,

the Zelevinsky tensor product of
V
with itself.
Recall from
Section 1
that

V\odot V=\mathrm{Ind}_{\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{1}\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{1}}^{\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}}(V\otimes V)=\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}\otimes_{\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{1}\otimes\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{1}}(V\otimes V).

Recall also that

\psi_{1,1}(\rho_{L}\otimes 1)=\rho T_{1},\quad\psi_{1,1}(1\otimes\rho_{R})=T_{1}^{-1}\rho,\quad\psi_{1,1}(\rho_{L}\otimes\rho_{R})=\rho^{2},

where
\rho\in\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
.
Thus, for any
r,s\in\mathbb{Z}
, we have

\psi_{1,1}(\rho_{L}^{r}\otimes\rho_{R}^{s})=(\rho T_{1})^{r}(T_{1}^{-1}\rho)^{s}.

This implies that
W
is two-dimensional and that
\{w,w^{\prime}\}
, where

(124)

w:=1\otimes v\otimes v\quad\text{and}\quad w^{\prime}:=\rho\otimes v\otimes v,

is a basis of
W
, on which the action of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
is given by
the matrices

(125)

[\rho]=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad[T_{1}]=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\
1&q^{-1}-q\end{pmatrix},\quad[T_{0}]=[\rho T_{0}\rho^{-1}]=\begin{pmatrix}q^{-1}-q&1\\
1&0\end{pmatrix}.

On the KL-basis, the action thus becomes

(126)

[b_{1}]=[T_{1}+q]=\begin{pmatrix}q&1\\
1&q^{-1}\end{pmatrix},\quad[b_{0}]=[T_{0}+q]=\begin{pmatrix}q^{-1}&1\\
1&q\end{pmatrix}.

Using the rules for multiplication w.r.t. the KL-basis, we see that the action matrices satisfy:

[b_{\widehat{2r}_{\,0}}]=r[b_{1}][b_{0}],\;[b_{\widehat{2r+1}_{\,1}}]=(2r+1)[b_{1}],\;[b_{\widehat{2r}_{\,1}}]=r[b_{0}][b_{1}],\;[b_{\widehat{2r+1}_{\,0}}]=(2r+1)[b_{0}],\;r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}.

Recall that
q
is a formal invertible parameter and let
{-}^{\mathbb{C}(q)}:={-}\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}]}\mathbb{C}(q)
. The following result is well-known, see e.g.
[
LNT
, Theorem 1]
.

Proposition 5.2
.

The
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext},\mathbb{C}(q)}_{2}
-module
W^{\mathbb{C}(q)}
is simple.

There is also an infinite dimensional
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
-module
U
which is closely related to
W
and whose categorification
will be important below. By definition,

U:=\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}/I,

the quotient of the regular left
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
-module by the left ideal
I
generated by

(127)

\rho^{2}-1\quad\text{and}\quad b_{1}\rho-q^{-1}b_{1}.

Remark 5.3
.

We stress that
I
is only a left ideal and not a two-sided ideal. For
\rho^{2}-1
this distinction is irrelevant, because
\rho^{2}
and
1
both belong to the center of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
, but for
b_{1}\rho-q^{-1}b_{1}
it matters. For example, the element
(1-q^{-2})b_{1}
belongs to the two-sided ideal generated by the elements in (
127
) because

(1-q^{-2})b_{1}=(b_{1}\rho-q^{-1}b_{1})(\rho+q^{-1})-b_{1}(\rho^{2}-1),

but it does not belong to
I
.

Proposition 5.4
.

Let
\pi_{U}\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}\to U
be the natural projection and define
u_{k}:=\pi_{U}(b_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}})
and
u^{\prime}_{k}:=\pi_{U}(\rho b_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}})
, for
all
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
. Then
\{u_{k},u^{\prime}_{k}\mid k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\}
is a basis of
U
and the action of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
on this basis is determined by

(128)

\begin{gathered}\rho u_{k-1}=u^{\prime}_{k-1},\quad\rho u^{\prime}_{k-1}=u_{k-1}\\
b_{1}u_{0}=u_{1},\quad b_{1}u_{2k}=u_{2k+1}+u_{2k-1},\quad b_{1}u_{2k-1}=[2]u_{2k-1},\\
b_{0}u_{0}=q^{-1}u^{\prime}_{1},\quad b_{0}u_{1}=u_{2},\quad b_{0}u_{2k}=[2]u_{2k},\quad b_{0}u_{2k+1}=u_{2k+2}+u_{2k},\\
b_{1}u^{\prime}_{0}=q^{-1}u_{1},\quad b_{1}u^{\prime}_{1}=u^{\prime}_{2},\quad b_{1}u^{\prime}_{2k}=[2]u^{\prime}_{2k},\quad b_{1}u^{\prime}_{2k+1}=u^{\prime}_{2k+2}+u^{\prime}_{2k},\\
b_{0}u^{\prime}_{0}=u^{\prime}_{1},\quad b_{0}u^{\prime}_{2k}=u^{\prime}_{2k+1}+u^{\prime}_{2k-1},\quad b_{0}u^{\prime}_{2k-1}=[2]u^{\prime}_{2k-1},\end{gathered}

for
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}
.

Proof.

To show that
\{u_{k},u^{\prime}_{k}\mid k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\}
spans
U
is easy. The KL-basis of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}/\langle\rho^{2}-1\rangle
,
where
\langle\rho^{2}-1\rangle
is the (left) ideal generated by
\rho^{2}-1
, is given by

\{\rho^{m}b_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}},\rho^{m}b_{\widehat{k}_{\,0}}\mid m\in\{0,1\},k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\}
. The images of those elements under
\pi_{U}
, therefore,
span
U
. By induction, it’s easy to show that
b_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\rho-q^{-1}b_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\in I
for all
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
. For
k=2
, we have

b_{01}-q^{-1}b_{01}=b_{0}(b_{1}\rho-q^{-1}b_{1})\in I

For
k>2
, induction yields

b_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\rho-q^{-1}b_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}=\begin{cases}b_{0}(b_{\widehat{k-1}_{\,1}}\rho-q^{-1}b_{\widehat{k-1}_{\,1}})-(b_{\widehat{k-2}_{\,1}}\rho-q^{-1}b_{\widehat{k-2}_{\,1}})\in I,&\text{if $k$ is even};\\
b_{1}(b_{\widehat{k-1}_{\,1}}\rho-q^{-1}b_{\widehat{k-1}_{\,1}})-(b_{\widehat{k-2}_{\,1}}\rho-q^{-1}b_{\widehat{k-2}_{\,1}})\in I,&\text{if $k$ is odd}.\end{cases}

This shows that
\rho b_{\widehat{k}_{\,0}}=b_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\rho=q^{-1}b_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}
in
U
, for all
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
. This in turn implies that
b_{\widehat{k}_{\,0}}=\rho^{2}b_{\widehat{k}_{\,0}}=q^{-1}\rho b_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}
, for all
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, which completes
the proof that
\{u_{k},u^{\prime}_{k}\mid k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\}
spans
U
.

It remains to prove that the elements
u_{k},u^{\prime}_{k}
, for
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, are all linearly independent in
U
. Suppose that

\lambda_{m_{1}}u_{m_{1}}+\ldots+\lambda_{m_{r}}u_{m_{r}}+\mu_{n_{1}}u^{\prime}_{n_{1}}+\ldots+\mu_{n_{s}}u^{\prime}_{n_{s}}=0\;\,\text{in $U$},

for some
r,s\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
and some
\mu_{m_{1}},\ldots,\mu_{m_{r}},\nu_{n_{1}}\ldots,\nu_{n_{s}}\in\Bbbk
. Then

(129)

\lambda_{m_{1}}b_{\widehat{m_{1}}_{\,1}}+\ldots+\lambda_{m_{r}}b_{\widehat{m_{r}}_{\,1}}+\mu_{n_{1}}\rho b_{\widehat{n_{1}}_{\,1}}+\ldots+\mu_{n_{s}}\rho b_{\widehat{n_{s}}_{\,1}}\in I.

Since
b_{1}\rho=\rho b_{0}
, any non-zero element in
I
will be a linear
combination of KL basis elements containing at least a non-zero multiple of

\rho b_{\widehat{k}_{\,0}}
, for some
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
, or
a non-zero multiple of
\rho^{2}b_{\widehat{k}_{\,i}}
,
for some
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
and
i\in\{0,1\}
. Either way, linear independence of the KL basis elements in
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
implies that (
129
) can only hold if
\lambda_{m_{1}}b_{\widehat{m_{1}}_{\,1}}+\ldots+\lambda_{m_{r}}b_{\widehat{m_{r}}_{\,1}}+\mu_{n_{1}}\rho b_{\widehat{n_{1}}_{\,1}}+\ldots+\mu_{n_{s}}\rho b_{\widehat{n_{s}}_{\,1}}=0
and, therefore,
that
\lambda_{m_{i}}=\mu_{n_{j}}=0
for all
i=1,\ldots,r
and
j=1,\ldots,s
.
This completes the proof that the elements
u_{k},u^{\prime}_{k}
, for
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, are all linearly independent in
U
.

Finally, it is easy to determine the action of
\rho,b_{0}
and
b_{1}
on this basis using the KL multiplication rules, because
\pi_{U}
is a morphism of

\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
-modules.
∎

Let
J\subset U
be the
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
-submodule generated by
T_{1}u_{0}-\rho u_{0}
and let
\overline{u}\in U/J
be the image of
u\in U

under the natural projection
U\to U/J
. We have

\displaystyle\overline{T_{1}u_{0}}=\overline{\rho u_{0}}=\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}},

\displaystyle\overline{T_{1}u^{\prime}_{0}}=\overline{T_{1}^{2}u_{0}}=\overline{(q^{-1}-q)T_{1}u_{0}+u_{0}}=\overline{(q^{-1}-q)u^{\prime}_{0}+u_{0}}.

Proposition 5.5
.

There is a surjective morphism of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
-modules

\pi^{U}_{W}\colon U\to W

and
\ker(\pi^{U}_{W})=J
.

Proof.

Define
\pi^{U}_{W}\colon U\to W
by

\pi^{U}_{W}(u_{0}):=w,

extending it to the whole of
U
by the requirement that it be a morphism of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
-modules.
Note that the matrices in (
126
) imply that

\displaystyle\pi^{U}_{W}(u^{\prime}_{0})=\pi^{U}_{W}(\rho u_{0})=\rho\pi^{U}_{W}(u_{0})=\rho w=w^{\prime};

\displaystyle\pi^{U}_{W}(b_{1}\rho u_{0})=b_{1}\pi^{U}_{W}(u^{\prime}_{0})=b_{1}w^{\prime}=w+q^{-1}w^{\prime}=q^{-1}b_{1}w=q^{-1}\phi_{J}(b_{1}u_{0}),

so
\pi^{U}_{W}
is well-defined.

The fact that
\pi^{U}_{W}(u_{0})=w
and
\pi^{U}_{W}(u^{\prime}_{0})=w^{\prime}
proves that
\pi^{U}_{W}
is surjective.

It remains to show that
\ker(\pi^{U}_{W})=J
. The matrices in
(
126
) show that
\rho T_{1}w=w
, which implies that

\pi^{U}_{W}(\rho T_{1}u_{0})=\rho T_{1}\pi^{U}_{W}(u_{0})=\rho T_{1}w=w=\pi^{U}_{W}(u_{0}),

so
J\subseteq\ker(\pi^{U}_{W})
. To prove that this inclusion is an equality we will show that

\dim_{\Bbbk}(U/J)=2
, which amounts to showing that
\overline{u_{k}},\overline{u^{\prime}_{k}}\in\mathrm{span}\{\overline{u_{0}},\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}}\}
for all
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
. We will prove this by induction.
Recall that
b_{i}=T_{i}+q
, for
i\in\{0,1\}
. Then, for the base step, we have

\displaystyle\overline{u_{1}}=\overline{b_{1}u_{0}}=\overline{T_{1}u_{0}+qu_{0}}=\overline{\rho u_{0}+qu_{0}}=\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}+qu_{0}},

\displaystyle\overline{u^{\prime}_{1}}=\overline{\rho u_{1}}=\overline{\rho u^{\prime}_{0}+q\rho u_{0}}=\overline{u_{0}+qu^{\prime}_{0}},

\displaystyle\overline{u_{2}}=\overline{b_{0}u_{1}}=\overline{b_{0}(u^{\prime}_{0}+qu_{0})}=2\overline{u^{\prime}_{1}}=2(\overline{u_{0}+qu^{\prime}_{0}}),

\displaystyle\overline{u^{\prime}_{2}}=\overline{\rho u_{2}}=2\overline{u_{1}}=2(\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}+qu_{0}}).

For the inductive step, let
k>2
and assume that
that
\overline{u_{m}},\overline{u^{\prime}_{m}}\in\mathrm{span}\{\overline{u_{0}},\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}}\}
for all
0\leq m<k
. If
k>2
is odd, then

\overline{u_{k}}=\overline{b_{1}u_{k-1}-u_{k-2}}.

By induction, the elements
\overline{u_{k-1}},\overline{u_{k-2}}
belong to
\mathrm{span}\{\overline{u_{0}},\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}}\}
. Since

\overline{b_{1}u_{0}}=\overline{u_{1}}=\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}+qu_{0}}
and
\overline{b_{1}u^{\prime}_{0}}=q^{-1}\overline{u_{1}}=\overline{q^{-1}u^{\prime}_{0}+u_{0}}
, we conclude
that
\overline{u_{k}}\in\mathrm{span}\{\overline{u_{0}},\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}}\}
. If
k>2
is even, then

\overline{u_{k}}=\overline{b_{0}u_{k-1}-u_{k-2}}.

By induction again, the elements
\overline{u_{k-1}},\overline{u_{k-2}}
belong to
\mathrm{span}\{\overline{u_{0}},\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}}\}
. Since

\overline{b_{0}u_{0}}=\overline{q^{-1}u^{\prime}_{1}}=\overline{q^{-1}u_{0}+u^{\prime}_{0}}
and
\overline{b_{0}u^{\prime}_{0}}=\overline{u^{\prime}_{1}}=\overline{u_{0}+qu^{\prime}_{0}}
, we conclude
that
\overline{u_{k}}\in\mathrm{span}\{\overline{u_{0}},\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}}\}
. This completes the proof that
u_{k}
belongs to
\mathrm{span}\{\overline{u_{0}},\overline{u^{\prime}_{0}}\}
for all
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
. Using similar arguments, one can show that the same also holds for
u^{\prime}_{k}
, for all
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, which concludes the proof.
∎

Just to fix notation, let
\pi_{W}\colon\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}\to W
be the projection of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
-modules defined by
\pi_{W}(x):=xw
, for any
x\in\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
. Then there is a commutative triangle

(130)

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces U}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{U}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi_{W}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi^{U}_{W}}

Remark 5.6
.

The infinite dimensional representation
U
of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
is the decategorification of a wide finitary birepresentation
\mathbf{U}
of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
, which appears naturally as the wide finitary cover of the induced birepresentation
\mathbf{W}
in
Section 5.3
.
However, we do not know if
U
also appears naturally in any approach to the representation theory of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
that does not use categorification. Note that this contrasts with the finitary cover
\widehat{\mathbf{M}}_{r,s}
(
r,s\in\mathbb{Z}
) of the evaluation birepresentation
\mathbf{M}^{\mathcal{E}v_{r,s}}
of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
in
[
MMV
, Corollary 6.5]
,
which decategorifies to a Graham-Lehrer cell module of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
, see
[
MMV
, Remark 6.6]
.

5.2.
Completions of linear additive categories

In this subsection, which is more abstract and general than the other subsections, we work over an arbitrary field
\Bbbk
. For the same reason,
the setting in the last subsubsection is that of general 2-categories and not restricted to monoidal categories (one-object 2-categories).

5.2.1.
Coproduct completions of additive
\Bbbk
-linear categories

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an additive
\Bbbk
-linear category.
Recall that the
additive closure

\operatorname{add}(\mathcal{A})
of a full subcategory
\mathcal{A}
of
\mathcal{C}
is the closure under direct sums and direct summands in
\mathcal{C}
.

We note that
\operatorname{Vect}_{\Bbbk}
is complete and cocomplete with respect to small weighted (and hence, in particular, conical) limits and colimits. This follows from
[
Rie
, Corollary 7.6.4]
using
[
Rie
, Example 3.7.5]
and the fact that
\operatorname{Vect}_{\Bbbk}
is enriched over itself.

This implies that the category of
\Bbbk
-linear functors
{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}={\sf{F}}un_{\Bbbk}(\mathcal{C}^{op},\operatorname{Vect}_{\Bbbk})
, is also (co)complete under weighted (co)limits by
[
Kel
, Section 3.3]
with (co)limits being computed object-wise. As usual, we identify an object
X
in
\mathcal{C}
with their representables
X^{\vee}=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(-,X)
under the Yoneda embedding. We denote by
\mathcal{C}^{\vee}
the image of
\mathcal{C}
under this embedding (which is, of course, equivalent to
\mathcal{C}
).

Note that we can realise a (co)product indexed by a set
J
as the conical (co)limit over the diagram
J\to\mathcal{C}\colon j\mapsto X_{j}
. This is a special case of the weighted (co)limit of the
\operatorname{Vect}_{\Bbbk}
-enriched functor
\tilde{J}\to\mathcal{C}
where
\tilde{J}
is the free
\operatorname{Vect}_{\Bbbk}
-enriched category on
J
and the weight
\tilde{J}\to\operatorname{Vect}_{\Bbbk}
is just the constant functor
j\mapsto\Bbbk
. For a family of objects
(X_{j})_{j\in J}
in
\mathcal{C}
, we slightly abuse notation by writing
\coprod_{j\in J}X_{j}
for said colimit in
{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}
rather than the formally correct
\coprod_{j\in J}X_{j}^{\vee}
and likewise for products.

Since
\mathcal{C}
and hence
{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}
is additive, in particular has a zero object, there is always a canonical monomorphism

\nu_{(X_{j})_{j\in J}}\colon\coprod_{j\in J}X_{j}\to\prod_{j\in J}X_{j}.

Explicitly, denoting by
\pi_{i}\colon\prod_{j\in J}X_{j}\to X_{i}
and
\iota_{i}\colon X_{i}\to\coprod_{j\in J}X_{j}
the canonical projections and injections, respectively,
\nu
is defined by the condition that

\pi_{i}\nu\iota_{k}=\begin{cases}\id_{X_{i}}&\text{if }i=k,\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

We define
{\mathcal{C}}^{\sqcup}
as the full subcategory of
{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}
where we close
\mathcal{C}^{\vee}
under countable coproducts.
We then denote by
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}=({\mathcal{C}}^{\sqcup})_{e}
its Karoubi envelope.
Note that both are again additive
\Bbbk
-linear categories. Moreover,
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}
is closed under countable coproducts. We observe that, by
[
Bre
, Theorem 4.1]
,
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}
and

{\mathcal{C}}^{\sqcup}
coincide provided
\mathcal{C}
is Krull-Schmidt.

A
\Bbbk
-linear functor
\mathrm{F}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
between additive
\Bbbk
-linear categories induces
\Bbbk
-linear functors, also denoted by
\mathrm{F}
, from
{\mathcal{C}}^{\sqcup}\to{\mathcal{D}}^{\sqcup}
, sending an object
\coprod_{j\in J}X_{j}
to
\coprod_{j\in J}\mathrm{F}(X_{j})
, and hence from
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}\to{\mathcal{D}}^{\diamond}
.

The next lemma will be crucial for computing morphism spaces in explicit examples.

Lemma 5.7
.

Assume
Y=\coprod_{j\in J}Y_{j}\in{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}
, where each
Y_{j}\in\mathcal{C}
. Let
X\in\mathcal{C}
and assume that
\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y_{j})=0
for all but finitely many
j\in J
. Then
\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}(X,Y)=\coprod_{j\in J}\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y_{j})
.

Proof.

Consider the natural monomorphism

\coprod_{j\in J}\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}(X,Y_{j})\xrightarrow{\kappa}\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}(X,\coprod_{j\in J}Y_{j})

and compose this with the monomorphism induced by
\nu=\nu_{(Y_{j})_{j\in J}},
i.e.

\coprod_{j\in J}\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}(X,Y_{j})\xrightarrow{\kappa}\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}(X,\coprod_{j\in J}Y_{j})\xrightarrow{\nu\circ-}\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}(X,\prod_{j\in J}Y_{j})\cong\prod_{j\in J}\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}(X,Y_{j})

The coproduct in the domain and the product in the codomain are both finite and hence isomorphic, so this monomorphism is an isomorphism. In particular,
\kappa
is an isomorphism. The lemma now follows from the fact that
\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}(X,Y_{j})=\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathcal{C}}(X,Y_{j})
by the Yoneda Lemma.
∎

Given that the (co)product of the morphism spaces in
Lemma 5.7
is really finite, we write it as

\bigoplus_{j\in J}\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}}(X,Y_{j}).

5.2.2.
Coproduct completions and homotopy categories

For a
\Bbbk
-linear additive category
\mathcal{C}
, we can consider the category
C^{b}(\mathcal{C})
of bounded complexes over
\mathcal{C}
and its completion
{C^{b}(\mathcal{C})}^{\sqcup}
under countable coproducts, and the Karoubi envelope
{C^{b}(\mathcal{C})}^{\diamond}
of the latter. Similarly, we can consider
C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\sqcup})
and
C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
.

For reference, we record the following lemma, for which we could not find a proof in the literature.

Lemma 5.8
.

For an idempotent complete
\Bbbk
-linear additive category
\mathcal{C}
, the category
C^{b}(\mathcal{C})
is idempotent complete.

Proof.

Assume
e^{\bullet}
is an idempotent endomorphism of an object
(X^{\bullet},d^{\bullet})
in
C^{b}(\mathcal{C})
. In particular, each
e^{i}
is an idempotent endormorphism of
X^{i}
. Since
\mathcal{C}
is idempotent complete,
X^{i}
splits into a direct sum of object
X^{i}_{e}
and
X^{i}_{1-e}
. Since
e^{\bullet}
commutes with the differential
d^{\bullet}
, each of these summands is preserved under the differential and the complex
(X^{\bullet},d^{\bullet})
splits into a direct sum of complexes
(X_{e}^{\bullet},e^{\bullet}d^{\bullet}e^{\bullet})
and
(X^{\bullet},(1-e)^{\bullet}d^{\bullet}(1-e)^{\bullet})
.
∎

Note that the Yoneda embedding
\mathcal{C}\xrightarrow{\Upsilon}{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}
extends to an embedding
C^{b}(\mathcal{C})\hookrightarrow C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
, which gives rise to an embedding
{C^{b}(\mathcal{C})}^{\diamond}\hookrightarrow{C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})}^{\diamond}
. The following lemma is straightforward, noticing that a countable coproduct of complexes, which each have countable coproducts of objects in each component, is again a complex with countable coproducts in each component.

Lemma 5.9
.

C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
is closed under countable coproducts, thus
C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})\simeq{C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})}^{\diamond}
and we have an embedding
\iota\colon{C^{b}(\mathcal{C})}^{\diamond}\hookrightarrow C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
.

Proof.

Let
(X_{i}^{\bullet},d_{i}^{\bullet})_{i\in I}
be a family of objects in
C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
and consider the coproduct
X=\coprod_{i\in I}(X_{i}^{\bullet},d_{i}^{\bullet})
in
{C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})}^{\sqcup}
. Now define
Y=(Y^{\bullet},d^{\bullet})
in
C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
as the complex whose
k
th component is given by
\coprod_{i\in I}X_{i}^{k}
and whose differential
d^{k}
is given by
\coprod_{i\in I}X_{i}^{k}\xrightarrow{(d_{i}^{k})_{i\in I}}\coprod_{i\in I}X_{i}^{k+1}
. Then clearly,
Y\cong X
, so
C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
is closed under coproducts and
C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})\simeq{C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})}^{\sqcup}
. Since by
Lemma 5.8
,
C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
is idempotent complete,
C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})\simeq{C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})}^{\diamond}
.
∎

Denote by
N^{b}(\mathcal{C})\subset C^{b}(\mathcal{C})
the ideal of nulhomotopic morphisms of complexes, and by
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})=C^{b}(\mathcal{C})/N^{b}(\mathcal{C})
the bounded homotopy category.

Observe that the faithful functor
C^{b}(\mathcal{C})\hookrightarrow C^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
induced by the Yoneda embedding preserves nullhomotopic maps, and we thus obtain a faithful functor
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})\hookrightarrow K^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
. Morover,
\iota
also preserves nullhomotopic morphisms so we also obtain a faithful functor
{K^{b}(\mathcal{C})}^{\diamond}\to K^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
, which we again denote by
\iota
.

Corollary 5.10
.

(1)

We have fully faithful functors
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})\xrightarrow{K^{b}(\Upsilon)}{K^{b}(\mathcal{C})}^{\diamond}\xrightarrow{\iota}K^{b}({\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond})
.

(2)

If
\mathcal{D}
is a
\Bbbk
-linear additive category, a
\Bbbk
-linear functor
\Phi\colon\mathcal{C}\to K^{b}(\mathcal{D})
induces a
\Bbbk
-linear functor
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}\to K^{b}({\mathcal{D}}^{\diamond})
.

Proof.

The first part is immediate. For the second part, note that
\Phi
gives rise to a functor
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}\to{K^{b}(\mathcal{D})}^{\diamond}
. Composing this with the inclusion from the first part yields the desired functor
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}\to K^{b}({\mathcal{D}}^{\diamond})
.
∎

5.2.3.
Wide finitary bicategories

Here we recall some of the definitions from
[
Macph
]
.

We denote by
\mathfrak{A}_{\Bbbk}
the
2
-category whose objects are additive
\Bbbk
-linear categories, whose
1
-morphisms are
\Bbbk
-linear functors and whose
2
-morphisms are natural transformations.

A category
\mathcal{C}
is
wide finitary
if it is an additive
\Bbbk
-linear Krull–Schmidt
category with at most countably many isomorphism classes of indecomposable objects and morphism spaces of at most countable dimension. We denote by
\ind{\mathcal{C}}
a set of representatives of isomorphism classes of indecomposable objects in
\mathcal{C}
.

We denote the
2
-category whose objects are wide finitary categories, whose
1
-morphisms are
\Bbbk
-linear functors, and whose
2
-morphisms are natural transformations by
\mathfrak{A}^{wf}_{\Bbbk}
.

We say that a bicategory
\mathcal{C}
is
wide finitary
if

•

it has finitely many objects;

•

\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})
is in
\mathfrak{A}^{wf}_{\Bbbk}
for all
\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j}\in\mathcal{C}
;

•

horizontal composition is biadditive and
\Bbbk
-linear;

•

the identity
1
-morphism
\mathbbm{1}_{\mathtt{i}}
is indecomposable for any
\mathtt{i}\in\mathcal{C}
.

We use
\circ_{\mathsf{h}}
, resp.
\circ_{\mathsf{v}}
, for horizontal, respectively vertical, composition in a bicategory.

A wide finitary bicategory
\mathcal{C}
is said to be
wide fiat
if there exists a weak involution
(-)^{*}\colon\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}^{\mathsf{co},\mathsf{op}}
such that, for any
1
-morphism
\mathrm{F}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})
, there are
natural
2
-morphisms
\alpha\colon\mathrm{F}\mathrm{F}^{*}\to\mathbbm{1}_{\mathtt{j}},\beta\colon\mathbbm{1}_{\mathtt{i}}\colon\mathrm{F}^{*}\mathrm{F}
satisfying the usual adjunction triangles, i.e.
(\alpha\circ_{0}\id_{\mathrm{F}})\circ_{1}(\id_{\mathrm{F}}\circ_{0}\beta)=\id_{\mathrm{F}}
and
(\beta\circ_{0}\id_{\mathrm{F}^{*}})\circ_{1}(\id_{\mathrm{F}^{*}}\circ_{0}\alpha)=\id_{\mathrm{F}^{*}}
.

Note that
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n}
is a wide fiat bicategory.

5.2.4.
Completed and triangulated bicategories.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a wide finitary bicategory. We define the bicategory
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}
to be the bicategory on the same objects as
\mathcal{C}
, but with morphism categories
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})={\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})}^{\diamond}(={\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})}^{\sqcup})
, with horizontal composition given component-wise, i.e.

\coprod_{i\in I}\mathrm{X}_{i}\coprod_{j\in J}\mathrm{Y}_{j}=\coprod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in I\\
j\in J\end{subarray}}\mathrm{X}_{i}\mathrm{Y}_{j}

and similarly for 2-morphisms. Observe that
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}
is locally additive and
\Bbbk
-linear.

Remark 5.11
.

Note that this naturally embeds into the completion
{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}
with morphism categories
{\mathcal{C}}^{\circ}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})={\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})}^{\circ}
and horizontal composition given by Day convolution.

Likewise, for any locally additive
\Bbbk
-linear (or in particular wide finitary) bicategory
\mathcal{C}
, we can define
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})
as having the same objects as
\mathcal{C}
, morphism categories
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})=K^{b}(\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j}))
and horizontal composition induced by taking the total complex of the tensor product of complexes. This is a triangulated bicategory, which fits within the bicategorical version of the framework considered in
[
LaMi
, Section 3.1]
.

Lemma 5.12
.

If
\mathcal{C}
is wide finitary and all
1
-morphisms have finite-dimensional endomorphism rings, then
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})
is wide finitary.

Proof.

Since
\mathcal{C}
is locally idempotent complete, so is
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})
by
[
Sch
, Theorem 3.4]
. Since endomorphism rings of
1
-morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
are finite-dimensional, the same is true for endomorphism rings of
1
-morphisms in
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})
. Thus
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})
is Krull-Schmidt by
[
Kra
, Cor 4.4]
. Countability of isomorphism classes of indecomposables is inherited from
\mathcal{C}
.
∎

Corollary 5.13
.

For any
n\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}
, the monoidal category (one-object bicategory)
K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{n})
is wide finitary.

5.2.5.
Birepresentations

An
additive birepresentation
of a locally additive
\Bbbk
-linear bicategory
\mathcal{C}
is a
\Bbbk
-linear pseudofunctor from
\mathcal{C}
to
\mathfrak{A}_{\Bbbk}
.
A
wide finitary birepresentation
of a wide finitary bicategory
\mathcal{C}
is a
\Bbbk
-linear pseudofunctor from
\mathcal{C}
to
\mathfrak{A}^{wf}_{\Bbbk}
.

We can extend an additive or wide finitary birepresentation
\mathbf{M}
of
\mathcal{C}
to an additive birepresentation
{\mathbf{M}}^{\diamond}
of
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}
by defining the action of
\mathrm{F}=\coprod_{i\in I}\mathrm{F}_{i}\in{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})
on
X=\coprod_{j\in J}X_{j}\in{\mathbf{M}}^{\diamond}(\mathtt{i})
componentwise, i.e.

\coprod_{i\in I}{\mathbf{M}}^{\diamond}(\mathrm{F}_{i})\coprod_{j\in J}X_{j}=\coprod_{\begin{subarray}{c}i\in I\\
j\in J\end{subarray}}{\mathbf{M}}^{\diamond}(\mathrm{F}_{i})X_{j}.

Similarly, any additive birepresentation of
\mathbf{M}
gives rise to a
triangulated
birepresentation
K^{b}(\mathbf{M})
of
K^{b}(\mathcal{C})
where
K^{b}(\mathbf{M})(\mathtt{i})=K^{b}(\mathbf{M}(\mathtt{i}))
.

5.2.6.
Algebras and birepresentations in
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a wide finitary bicategory.

Now assume
G
is an abelian group and
\mathrm{Y}=\coprod_{j\in G}\mathrm{Y}_{j}\in{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})
is an algebra
1
-morphism with product

\mathbf{m}\colon\coprod_{i,j\in G}\mathrm{Y}_{i}\mathrm{Y}_{j}\to\coprod_{k\in G}\mathrm{Y}_{k}

determined by component morphisms
\mathbf{m}_{i,j}=\mathbf{m}(\iota_{i}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\iota_{j})\colon\mathrm{Y}_{i}\mathrm{Y}_{j}\to\mathrm{Y}_{i+j}
, where we identify
\mathrm{Y}_{i+j}
with the subobject of
\coprod_{k\in G}\mathrm{Y}_{k}
given by
\iota_{i+j}(\mathrm{Y}_{i+j})
, and unit
\mathbf{u}
determined by a morphism
\mathbbm{1}_{\mathtt{i}}\to\mathrm{Y}_{0}
, where
0
is the neutral element in
G
.

For each
\mathtt{j}\in\mathcal{C}
, we can consider the category of
\mathrm{Y}
-modules in
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})
, denoted by
\operatorname{mod}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})}^{\diamond}}\mathrm{Y}
, which gives rise to an additive birepresentation
\boldsymbol{\operatorname{mod}}_{{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}}\mathrm{Y}
of
{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}
. Note that each
\operatorname{mod}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})}^{\diamond}}\mathrm{Y}
is
idempotent complete by construction.

By the usual free forgetful adjunction, we have, for
\mathrm{F}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})
an isomorphism

(131)

\begin{array}[]{rcl}\mathrm{Hom}_{\operatorname{mod}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})}^{\diamond}}\mathrm{Y}}(\mathrm{F}\mathrm{Y},\mathrm{Y})&\cong&\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})}^{\diamond}}(\mathrm{F},\mathrm{Y})\\
f&\mapsto&f\circ_{\mathsf{v}}(\id_{\mathrm{F}}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\mathbf{u})\\
\mathbf{m}\circ_{\mathsf{v}}(g\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\id_{\mathrm{Y}})&\mapsfrom&g.\end{array}

Lemma 5.14
.

Let
\mathrm{Y}=\coprod_{j\in G}\mathrm{Y}_{j}\in{\mathcal{C}}^{\diamond}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})
be an algebra
1
-morphism as above,
\mathrm{F}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})
and
g\in\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})}^{\diamond}}(\mathrm{F},\mathrm{Y})
. Assume that
g
factors over
\iota_{j}
, i.e. there exists an
g_{j}\in\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})}}(\mathrm{F},\mathrm{Y}_{j})
such that
g=\iota_{j}\circ_{\mathsf{v}}g_{j}
. Then under the isomorphism in (
131
),
g
corresponds to a morphism
f
defined by

f\circ_{\mathsf{v}}(\id_{\mathrm{F}}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\iota_{k})=\mathbf{m}_{j,k}\circ_{\mathsf{v}}(g_{j}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\id_{\mathrm{Y}_{k}})\colon\mathrm{F}\mathrm{Y}_{k}\to\mathrm{Y}_{j+k}.

Proof.

This is a direct computation, observing that

\begin{split}f\circ_{\mathsf{v}}(\id_{\mathrm{F}}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\iota_{k})&=\mathbf{m}\circ_{\mathsf{v}}(g\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\id_{\mathrm{Y}})\circ_{\mathsf{v}}(\id_{\mathrm{F}}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\iota_{k})\\
&=\mathbf{m}\circ_{\mathsf{v}}((\iota_{j}\circ_{\mathsf{v}}g_{j})\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\iota_{k})\\
&=\mathbf{m}\circ_{\mathsf{v}}(\iota_{j}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\iota_{k})\circ_{\mathsf{v}}(g_{j}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\id_{\mathrm{Y}_{k}})\\
&=\mathbf{m}_{j,k}\circ_{\mathsf{v}}(g_{j}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\id_{\mathrm{Y}_{k}})\\
\end{split}

so the claim follows.
∎

Lemma 5.15
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a wide finitary bicategory and
\mathrm{Y}\in{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})}^{\diamond}
an algebra
1
-morphism. Assume that for any
\mathrm{G}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})
, the morphism space
\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})}^{\diamond}}(\mathrm{G},\mathrm{Y})
is finite-dimensional. Then the birepresentation
\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{Y}}
given by
\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{Y}}(\mathtt{j})=\operatorname{add}\{\mathrm{F}\mathrm{Y}\,|\,\mathrm{F}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})\}
(where the additive closure is taken in
\operatorname{mod}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})}^{\diamond}}\mathrm{Y}
) is wide finitary.

Proof.

By (
131
), for each
\mathrm{F}\in\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})
, the endomorphism ring
\mathrm{End}_{\operatorname{mod}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})}^{\diamond}}\mathrm{Y}}(\mathrm{F}\mathrm{Y})
is isomorphic to
\mathrm{Hom}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{i})}^{\diamond}}(\mathrm{F}^{*}\mathrm{F},\mathrm{Y})
, which by assumption is finite-dimensional. Since each
\operatorname{mod}_{{\mathcal{C}(\mathtt{i},\mathtt{j})}^{\diamond}}\mathrm{Y}
is idempotent complete,
[
Kra
, Cor 4.4]
implies that each
\mathbf{M}(\mathtt{j})
is Krull-Schmidt. Moreover, the number of isomorphism classes of indecomposable objects is countable and morphism spaces are even finite-dimensional, so
\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{Y}}
is wide finitary.
∎

5.3.
The categorified story

In the first part of this section, we will define a graded wide-finitary birepresentation
\mathbf{U}
of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
and show that it categorifies the representation
U
of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
. In the second part, we will define a triangulated birepresentation
\mathbf{W}
of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
and conjecture that it categorifies the representation
W
of
\widehat{H}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
.

5.3.1.
The categorification of
U

Let
\mathbf{V}
be the rank one finitary
2
-representation of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{1}
categorifying
V
. The corresponding algebra object

\mathrm{X}\in\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext},\diamond}_{1}
is given by

\mathrm{X}:=\coprod_{r\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{r},

with multiplication
\mu\colon\mathrm{X}\mathrm{X}\to\mathrm{X}
defined by the identity on
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{k}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{r-k}=\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{r}
, for all

r,k\in\mathbb{Z}
, and unit
\epsilon\colon\mathrm{I}\to\mathrm{X}
defined as the identity on
\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{0}
and zero to
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{r}
, for all

r\neq 0
. Note that
(\mathrm{B}_{\rho})^{k}\cong\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}
and
\mathrm{hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{1}}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}\langle s\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{m}}\langle t\rangle)\cong\delta_{s,t}\delta_{k,m}\mathbb{R}
, for any
k,m,s,t\in\mathbb{Z}
, where
\delta_{-,-}
is the Kronecker delta.

Consider
\mathrm{Y}:=\Psi_{1,1}(\mathrm{X}\boxtimes\mathrm{X})\in K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext},\diamond}_{2})
. The fact that
\Psi_{1,1}
is a monoidal functor
and the isomorphisms
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\boxtimes\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\cong(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\boxtimes\mathrm{I})(\mathrm{I}\boxtimes\mathrm{B}_{\rho})\cong(\mathrm{I}\otimes\mathrm{B}_{\rho})(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\boxtimes\mathrm{I})
imply that

\mathrm{Y}\cong\coprod_{r\in\mathbb{Z}}\coprod_{s\in\mathbb{Z}}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r}(\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho})^{s}\cong\coprod_{r\in\mathbb{Z}}\coprod_{s\in\mathbb{Z}}(\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho})^{s}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r}.

Note that, for any
k,l\in\mathbb{Z}
, there are natural isomorphisms

(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{k}\,(\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho})^{l}\,\mathrm{Y}\cong\mathrm{Y}\cong(\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho})^{l}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{k}\,\mathrm{Y},

because
(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{k}
and
(\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho})^{l}
commute and

(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{k}\,(\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho})^{l}\,\mathrm{Y}\cong\coprod_{r\in\mathbb{Z}}\coprod_{s\in\mathbb{Z}}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r+k}(\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho})^{s+l}\cong\mathrm{Y}.

In particular, we see that

(132)

\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1}\mathrm{Y}\cong\mathrm{Y},\quad\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{Y}\cong\mathrm{Y},\quad\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{2}\mathrm{Y}\cong\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1}\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{Y}\cong\mathrm{Y}.

For any
r,s\in\mathbb{Z}
, define

\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}:=(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r}(\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho})^{s}.

Lemma 5.16
.

Let
i\in\{0,1\}
, and
k,t\in\mathbb{Z}
, and
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
. Then

(133)

\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,i}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}\right)=0

for all but finitely many
r,s\in\mathbb{Z}
.

Proof.

By
[
MaTh
, Theorem 2.5]
, the hom-space in (
133
) is zero if
r+s\neq k
. Now, assume that
r+s=k
. We also assume that
r\geq k
, the case
r\leq k
being similar. Then

\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}=(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r}(\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{B}_{\rho})^{k-r}\cong(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{k}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r-k}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r-k}\cong\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{k}\mathrm{T}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}\cong\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}\mathrm{T}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}.

By biadjointness of
\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}
and
\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{-k}}
, we have

\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,i}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}\mathrm{T}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}\right)\cong\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,i}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{T}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}\right),

which in turn is isomorphic to

\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,i}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{T}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}^{\min}\right),

where
\mathrm{T}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}^{\min}
is the minimal complex obtained from
\mathrm{T}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}
by Gaussian elimination,
which is unique up to homotopy equivalence. By
[
ElWi1
, Theorem 6.9]
, the degree-zero cochain object of

\mathrm{T}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}^{\min}
is isomorphic to
\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}
, which implies that

\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,i}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{T}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}^{\min}\right)\right)\leq\dim_{\mathbb{R}}\left(\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,i}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{2r-k}_{\,1}}\right)\right).

For a fixed choice of
m,t\in\mathbb{Z}
and
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, Soergel’s hom formula and the equations in (
123
) imply that the latter morphism space is zero for all but finitely many
r\in\mathbb{Z}
, which proves the lemma.
∎

The following corollary is an immediate consequence of
Lemma 5.7
and
Lemma 5.16
.

Corollary 5.17
.

For any
i\in\{0,1\}
, and
k,t\in\mathbb{Z}
, and
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, there is an isomorphism

(134)

\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext},\diamond}_{2})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,i}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{Y}\right)\cong\bigoplus_{r,s\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}\left(\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{k}}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,i}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}\right).

We are now going to define a graded wide finitary birepresentation
\mathbf{U}
of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
and the rest of this section after the definition will be dedicated to the proof that it categorifies
U
.

Definition 5.18
.

Let

\mathbf{U}:=\mathbf{M}_{\mathrm{Y}}

be the wide finitary birepresentation of
\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}
generated by
\mathrm{Y}
, as defined in
Lemma 5.15
.

Lemma 5.7
and the isomorphism in (
131
)
imply that

(135)

\mathrm{hom}_{\mathrm{Y}}(\mathrm{A}\mathrm{Y},\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Y})\cong\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext},\diamond}_{2})}(\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Y})\cong\bigoplus_{r,s\in\mathbb{Z}}\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}(\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}),\quad\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\in\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2},

where for simplicity we write
\mathrm{hom}_{\mathrm{Y}}(\mathrm{A}\mathrm{Y},\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Y})=\mathrm{hom}_{\operatorname{mod}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext},\diamond}_{2})}\mathrm{Y}}(\mathrm{A}\mathrm{Y},\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Y})
.
The isomorphisms in (
135
) show that any morphism
f\in\mathrm{hom}_{\mathrm{Y}}(\mathrm{A}\mathrm{Y},\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Y})
is determined by its components

f^{r,s}\in\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}(\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s})
, for
r,s\in\mathbb{Z}
.
Suppose
f\colon\mathrm{A}\mathrm{Y}\to BY
and
g\colon\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Y}\to\mathrm{C}\mathrm{Y}
are such that their only nonzero components under the free forgetful adjunction are

f^{r,s}\colon\mathrm{A}\to\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}
and
g^{p,q}\colon\mathrm{B}\to\mathrm{C}\mathrm{Y}^{p,q}
.
Then the only nonzero component of
g\circ f\colon\mathrm{A}\mathrm{Y}\to\mathrm{C}\mathrm{Y}
under the free forgetful adjunction, is given by the composition

(136)

\mathrm{A}\xrightarrow{f^{r,s}}\mathrm{B}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}\xrightarrow{g^{p,q}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\id_{\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}}}\mathrm{C}\mathrm{Y}^{p,q}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}\xrightarrow{\id_{\mathrm{C}}\circ_{\mathsf{h}}\mathbf{m}}\mathrm{C}\mathrm{Y}^{p+r,q+s}.

For morphisms with multiple nonzero components, this extends additively.

Proposition 5.19
.

Let
k,m\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
and
r,s\in\mathbb{Z}
. When
r\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
, the morphism spaces

\displaystyle\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s})\;\,\text{and}\;\,\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,0}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s})

are both zero for all
t\geq 0
.

Proof.

We only prove the first case, the proof of the second one being similar. Biadjointness and the isomorphism
\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,1}}^{*}\cong\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}}
imply that

\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s})\cong\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}(\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}).

By
[
MaTh
, Theorem 2.5]
, that hom-space is zero if
r+s\neq 0
, so suppose that
r+s=0
. Then

\mathrm{Y}^{r,s}\cong(\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r}.

Let
r>0
. By
[
ElWi1
, Theorem 6.9]
(see also
[
EMTW
, Theorem 19.47]
), the minimal complex

[(\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r}]^{\mathrm{min}}
is of the form

(137)

\displaystyle\underline{\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{2r}_{\,1}}}\xlongrightarrow{\mathrm{d}^{0}}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{2r-1}_{\,0}}\langle 1\rangle\oplus\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{2r-1}_{\,1}}\langle 1\rangle\longrightarrow\ldots,

where the underlined cochain object has homological degree zero and the differential
\mathrm{d}^{0}
is given by

(138)

\mathrm{d}^{0}=\begin{pmatrix}\lx@xy@svg{\hbox{\raise 2.5pt\hbox{\kern 26.00708pt\hbox{{\hbox{\kern-26.00708pt\raise 0.14226pt\hbox{\hbox{\kern 0.0pt\raise-33.45007pt\hbox{$\textstyle{\hbox to52.01pt{\vbox to66.9pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 26.00708pt\lower-33.45007pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} {{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{

where
\mathrm{JW}_{(0,\ldots,1)}
is the idempotent in
\mathrm{end}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}}(\mathrm{B}_{0}\cdots\mathrm{B}_{1})
obtained from the Jones-Wenzl projector

\mathrm{JW}_{2r}
by the quantum Satake correspondence, as in
[
Eli1
, Section 5.3.2]
(see also
[
EMTW
, Section 9.3]
),
and
T
denotes the transpose. Note that Elias and Williamson do not give the multiplicities of the indecomposables in positive
homological degree, but in affine type
A_{1}

both multiplicities in homological degree one can be deduced from the corresponding coefficients in (
122
).
On the other hand, the formulas in (
123
) imply that the decomposition of
\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\langle t\rangle
only contains indecomposables of the form
\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}\langle t+v\rangle
, with
0\leq n\leq k+m
and
v\in\{-1,0,1\}
. The parity conditions for
{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,1}
amount to
n
being odd.
Any non-zero morphism of complexes in
\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}(\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\langle t\rangle,[(\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r}]^{\mathrm{min}})
is given by a non-zero morphism in the morphism space

\mathrm{hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}}(\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{m}}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{2r}_{\,1}})
that is annihilated by postcomposition with the differential
\mathrm{d}^{0}
. The latter morphism space is the direct sum of morphism spaces whose sources are the indecomposables
of the form
\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}\langle t+v\rangle
, with
0\leq n\leq k+m
and
v\in\{-1,0,1\}
, and Soergel’s hom formula in
(
49
) and
Lemma 5.1
imply that
the graded rank of
\mathrm{Hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext},*}_{2}}(\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,1}},\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{2r}_{\,1}})
is equal to

(139)

\left(b_{{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,1}},b_{{}_{0}\widehat{2r}_{\,1}}\right)=q^{|n-2r|}p^{\prime}(q),

where
p^{\prime}(q)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}[q]
has constant term equal to one. This implies that the morphism space

\mathrm{hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}}(\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{n}_{\,1}}\langle t+v\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{2r}_{\,1}})
is zero unless
t+v=-|n-2r|
. Suppose that

t\geq 0
and recall that
v\in\{-1,0,1\}
. Since
n
must be odd, we also see that
|n-2r|>0
, so
t+v=-|n-2r|
can only
hold if
t=0
,
v=-1
and
|n-2r|=1
. In other words, the only non-zero morphism spaces are

\mathrm{hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}}(\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{2r-1}_{\,1}}\langle-1\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{{}_{0}\widehat{2r}_{\,1}})\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{hom}_{\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2}}(\mathrm{B}_{{}_{1}\widehat{2r+1}_{\,1}}\langle-1\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{{}_{0}\widehat{2r}_{\,1}}),

which are both one-dimensional and generated by

(140)

respectively. However, neither of these two morphisms extends to a map of complexes whose

[(\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{r}]^{\mathrm{min}}
. To see this, note that postcomposition with

\mathrm{d}^{0}
adds an extra dot to the rightmost, resp. leftmost, top strand of the morphisms in (
140
). These morphisms are all
non-zero, because even with dots on all strands such morphisms are non-zero, see e.g.
[

, Section 5.3.4]

and

, (10.8i) and (10.9)]
.

\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\langle t\rangle,\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s})=0,\quad\text{if}\;\,r>0\;\text{and}\;t\geq 0.\qed

Corollary 5.20
.

For all
k\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}
, the objects
\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}
and
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}
are indecomposable in

\mathbf{U}
.

Proof.

The isomorphisms in (
135
) show that any non-zero idempotent

e\in\mathrm{hom}_{\mathrm{Y}}(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y},\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y})
is completely
determined by its components
e^{r,s}\in\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}},\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s})
, for
r,s\in\mathbb{Z}
,
and that only finitely many components are non-zero. By
[
MaTh
, Theorem 2.5]
and

Proposition 5.19
, we have
e^{r,s}=0
unless
r+s=0
and
r\leq 0
. Furthermore,
e^{0,0}
must be a multiple of
the identity on
\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}
, by Soergel’s hom formula in (
49
). By a slight abuse of notation, justified by

Lemma 5.14
, let us write
e=e^{r_{1},-r_{1}}+\ldots+e^{r_{m},-r_{m}}
, for some
r_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\leq 0}
and
m\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}
. Then
e^{2}=e
if and only if

(141)

\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i,j\leq m\\[0.90417pt]
r_{i}+r_{j}=r_{k}\end{subarray}}e^{r_{i},-r_{i}}\circ e^{r_{j},-r_{j}}=e^{r_{k},-r_{k}},\;\text{for all}\;1\leq k\leq m.

First, assume that
e^{0,0}=0
and let
r_{\max}
be the maximal
r\in\mathbb{Z}_{<0}
such that
e^{r,-r}\neq 0
. Then the equation in (
141
) for
r_{k}=r_{\max}
has no solution, which shows that
e^{2}=e
cannot hold.

Next, assume that
e^{0,0}\neq 0
. Without loss of
generality, we may assume that
r_{1}=0
and
r_{i}<0
for all
2\leq i\leq m
. Then the equations in (
141
) can only hold if

e^{0,0}=\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}}
and

(142)

\displaystyle e^{r_{k},-r_{k}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}i,j\in\{2,\ldots,\hat{k},\ldots,m\}\\[0.90417pt]
r_{i}+r_{j}=r_{k}\end{subarray}}e^{r_{i},-r_{i}}\circ e^{r_{j},-r_{j}}=0,\;\text{for all}\;2\leq k\leq m.

In turn, the equations in (
142
) can only hold if
e^{r_{k},-r_{k}}=0
for all
2\leq k\leq m
, as can be seen by first considering
the maximal
r_{k}<0
and then working one’s way down until the minimal
r_{k}<0
. This shows that
e^{2}=e
holds if and only if

e=\mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}}
, hence
\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}
is indecomposable in
\mathbf{U}
.

Since
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}^{*}\cong\mathrm{B}_{\rho^{-1}}
, we have

\mathrm{hom}_{\mathrm{Y}}(\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y},\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y})\cong\mathrm{hom}_{\mathrm{Y}}(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y},\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}),

which implies that
\mathrm{B}_{\rho}\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}
is also indecomposable in
\mathbf{U}
, by the arguments above.
∎

Remark 5.21
.

When
r<0
, the morphism space
\mathrm{hom}_{K^{b}(\widehat{\mathcal{S}}^{\mathrm{ext}}_{2})}(\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{k}_{\,1}},\mathrm{B}_{\widehat{m}_{\,1}}\mathrm{Y}^{r,s})
can be non-zero.
Take
k=m=2
and
r=-1
, for example. Then
\mathrm{Y}^{-1,+1}\cong(\mathrm{T}_{0}\mathrm{T}_{1})^{-1}\cong\mathrm{T}_{1}^{-1}\mathrm{T}_{0}^{-1}
